author: Fowler
title: Targeted Layer-wise Knowledge Transfer for Efficient Language Model Compression via Task-Relevant Feature Selection
abstract: Compressing large teacher models into compact student models is a well-established application of layer-wise distillation. In this paradigm, the student learns by reproducing the teacher's hidden representations across all intermediate layers. Despite its utility, layer-wise distillation presents notable challenges: the student's reduced model capacity frequently leads to underfitting, and the teacher's hidden representations carry redundant information that is not necessarily relevant to what the student must learn for the target task. We address both issues with the proposed method, which introduces task-aware filters applied at each layer to align the hidden representations of the student and teacher. By retaining only task-relevant knowledge from these representations, the proposed method narrows the gap between the two models, enabling the student to achieve a better fit on the target task. Experiments conducted under both continual pre-training and fine-tuning settings show that the proposed method yields substantial and consistent gains relative to existing distillation approaches across both scenarios. Code is released at https://github.com/cliang1453/task-aware-distillation.

author: Johnson
title: Reducing Gender Disparity in Student Language Models Through Counterfactual Role Reversal During Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation has made it feasible to deploy language models in resource-constrained environments, where they demonstrate strong capability in coherent text generation. Nevertheless, such models frequently exhibit biases, among them the unwarranted linking of gender-neutral occupations to either male or female genders. When knowledge distillation is applied without fairness-aware constraints, the student model risks inheriting or even amplifying the biases already present in the teacher model. To address this problem, we introduce a fairness-conscious training approach that mitigates gender disparity during the distillation process itself. Specifically, the proposed method contributes two modifications built on counterfactual role reversal: adjusting the teacher's output probabilities and expanding the training set through data augmentation. We measure gender polarity across a range of professions in open-ended text produced by the resulting distilled and finetuned GPT-2 models, finding a marked decrease in gender disparity accompanied by only a modest loss in utility. Additionally, our findings reveal that language models exhibiting reduced gender polarity in generation do not consequently improve embedding fairness or the fairness of downstream classification tasks.

author: Hill
title: Lifelong Learning in Minecraft Through a Hierarchical Deep Reinforcement Learning Framework
abstract: We introduce an architecture for lifelong learning that transfers and reuses knowledge across tasks while preserving previously acquired information. The proposed method operates within Minecraft, a widely played video game that constitutes a high-dimensional, as-yet-unsolved benchmark for lifelong learning. Transferable behaviors—termed Deep Skill Networks—are integrated into the proposed method's hierarchical structure via two mechanisms: (1) a deep skill array and (2) skill distillation, a novel adaptation of policy distillation (Rusu et al. 2015) tailored to skill acquisition. By consolidating multiple reusable skills into a single distilled network, skill distillation allows the proposed method to accumulate knowledge and scale effectively under lifelong learning conditions. Across several sub-domains of Minecraft, the proposed method demonstrates both superior performance and reduced sample complexity relative to the standard Deep Q Network (Mnih et al. 2015).

author: Walker
title: Meta Learning-Driven Knowledge Distillation: Teaching BERT to Transfer Better
abstract: Traditional knowledge distillation (KD) approaches keep the teacher network frozen throughout training; the proposed method offers a simple but effective alternative by enabling the teacher network to refine its knowledge transfer strategy through a meta learning framework, guided by feedback from the distilled student network's performance—an approach we term learning to teach. In addition, to address the misalignment that arises between the inner-learner and meta-learner in meta learning algorithms oriented toward inner-learner improvement, the proposed method incorporates a pilot update mechanism. Across a range of benchmarks, the proposed method demonstrates substantial gains over conventional KD algorithms. It also exhibits reduced sensitivity to variations in student capacity and hyperparameter selection, making the application of KD more practical across diverse tasks and model configurations.

author: Doyle
title: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Recommender Systems via Latent Knowledge and Relaxed Ranking
abstract: Knowledge distillation—a model compression technique that transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a compact student model—has recently been adopted by recommender systems to lower inference latency without sacrificing performance. Existing state-of-the-art approaches concentrate exclusively on training the student model to closely replicate the teacher's predictions, and suffer from the drawback that those predictions convey only a partial picture of what the teacher has learned. We introduce a novel knowledge distillation framework for recommender systems, the proposed method, in which the student learns not only from the teacher's predictions but also from the latent knowledge embedded within the teacher. The proposed method is composed of two components: 1) a Distillation Experts module that achieves direct transfer of the teacher's latent knowledge by leveraging "experts" together with a novel expert selection strategy, enabling effective distillation of the teacher's extensive knowledge into a capacity-limited student; and 2) a Relaxed Ranking Distillation module that transfers knowledge derived from the teacher's predictions by accounting for relaxed ranking orders across items. Through comprehensive experiments, the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art baselines and attains performance comparable to, or exceeding, that of the teacher model while delivering faster inference.

author: Rhodes
title: Knowledge Distillation for Continual Language Learning
abstract: Maintaining performance across a sequential stream of tasks in lifelong language learning (LLL) without degradation relative to multi-task counterparts remains a significant challenge. We propose a simple yet effective method, applicable to existing LLL architectures, that mitigates this degradation through knowledge distillation. When a new task is introduced, the proposed method first trains a dedicated teacher model on that task, then transfers the acquired knowledge to the LLL model via knowledge distillation over the logits and features of intermediate layers. This enables the LLL model to adapt effectively to the incoming task while preserving previously learned knowledge. Across both text classification and sequence generation tasks, experiments demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves upon prior state-of-the-art LLL models, substantially reducing the performance gap between LLL models and their multi-task counterparts.

author: Mcclain
title: Leveraging Internal Representations for Improved Knowledge Distillation
abstract: A common paradigm in knowledge distillation involves optimizing a compact student model to replicate the behavior of a large, heavyweight teacher model. The teacher's output probabilities serve as soft-labels that guide the student toward capturing the teacher's knowledge in compressed form. Yet when the teacher is substantially larger than the student, there is no guarantee that matching these soft-labels will cause the student's internal representations to align with those of the teacher; even strong agreement at the output level can coexist with considerable divergence in intermediate layers. Such misalignment in internal representations risks degrading the generalization ability that distillation was originally meant to convey. We therefore propose distilling the internal representations of a large model such as BERT into a smaller, reduced version of that model. Two distinct formulations for carrying out this internal-representation distillation are introduced, together with several algorithms for performing it in practice. Evaluations conducted across datasets from the GLUE benchmark consistently demonstrate that combining distillation from internal representations with soft-label distillation yields a more powerful approach than relying on soft-label distillation alone.

author: Miller
title: Enhancing Spoken Question Answering Performance Through a Knowledge Distillation Framework
abstract: Comprehending complex spoken documents to answer questions—the spoken question answering (SQA) problem—poses substantial difficulties for machines. A critical component shaping the quality of QA systems is automatic speech recognition (ASR). Nevertheless, recent findings indicate that ASR systems produce transcripts with considerable noise, severely constraining machine comprehension performance on SQA. To tackle this limitation, the proposed method introduces a distillation framework designed to transfer knowledge between spoken documents and their written counterparts. The core contribution is a training strategy in which a language model supplies supervision signals through knowledge distillation (KD), guiding the student toward higher accuracy by narrowing the gap between automatic and manual transcriptions. Evaluation on the Spoken-SQuAD dataset shows that the proposed method surpasses multiple state-of-the-art language models.

author: Henderson
title: Single-Network Distillation from Ensembles via Adversarial Training
abstract: Ensembles of multiple base-level deep neural networks frequently achieve the highest accuracy, yet storing and running many such networks at test-time is computationally prohibitive for large-scale settings such as ImageNet. We introduce a distillation framework that compresses knowledge from a collection of trained deep neural networks (DNNs) into one compact DNN. To transfer diverse knowledge from multiple teacher models, an adversarial-based learning strategy is employed: a block-wise training loss directs optimization of the predefined student network to recover teacher model knowledge, while a discriminator network is simultaneously trained to differentiate teacher features from student features. The proposed method offers three key benefits: (1) guided training with discriminators yields a student network that is optimized more effectively than the corresponding original model; (2) a single forward pass at inference achieves performance that surpasses even traditional multi-original-model ensembles; (3) the student network is capable of learning distilled knowledge from teacher models of arbitrary structure. We conduct extensive experiments on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, and ImageNet, confirming the effectiveness of the approach. On ImageNet, a ResNet-50 student trained with the proposed method attains top-1/5 validation errors of 21.79%/5.99%, outperforming the original model by 2.06%/1.14%. Code and models are publicly available at: https://github.com/AaronHeee/MEAL

author: Robinson
title: Teacher Network Optimization for Student-Aware Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We introduce an approach to knowledge distillation that reshapes how dark knowledge is transferred from a teacher to a student. Unlike the majority of prior work, which focuses on optimizing student models given fixed pretrained teachers, our method targets the teacher itself, training it to produce representations that are inherently more compatible with student models and therefore better suited for knowledge transfer. Concretely, during teacher model optimization, the proposed method jointly trains student branches alongside the teacher in order to arrive at student-friendly representations. Because the central contribution is in how teacher models are trained—with the subsequent knowledge distillation procedure remaining straightforward—most existing knowledge distillation methods can incorporate this technique to achieve gains in both accuracy and convergence speed across a wide variety of student models. Across several established knowledge distillation techniques and numerous teacher and student model pairings, the proposed method achieves superior accuracy, and this holds even when teacher and student architectures are heterogeneous and no prior knowledge about the student models is available at the time of teacher network training.

author: Wagner
title: Knowledge Distillation from a Model's Own Soft Targets for Natural Language Processing
abstract: Deep learning models have demonstrated striking results across numerous NLP tasks since becoming central to the field, in some instances surpassing human-level performance. This success is largely attributable to the effective way such models encode knowledge in their representations. Although various approaches have been explored for learning more efficient representations, knowledge distillation from pretrained deep networks has shown that soft target probabilities carry richer training signal than hard labels alone. We introduce a knowledge distillation approach in which the soft target probabilities generated by the model currently being trained serve as the distillation signal—multimode information is distilled from the word embedding space immediately preceding the softmax layer. To manage computational cost, the proposed method employs an approximation of these soft target probabilities. We evaluate the proposed method on two fundamental and distinct NLP tasks: language modeling and neural machine translation. Experimental results demonstrate consistent performance gains on both tasks.

author: Johnson
title: Theoretical Analysis of Knowledge Distillation in Wide Networks: Generalization Bounds, Training Difficulty, and Teacher Imperfection
abstract: A student network can be trained by leveraging soft output produced by a teacher network, a technique known as knowledge distillation that has proven effective for both model compression and knowledge transfer. Despite its empirical success, a rigorous theoretical foundation for knowledge distillation remains lacking. Meanwhile, advances in neural tangent kernel theory make it possible to approximate a wide neural network using a linear model built on the network's random features. We present a theoretical treatment of knowledge distillation applied to wide neural networks. We begin by deriving a transfer risk bound for the linearized network model. We then introduce a measure we term data inefficiency to quantify how difficult a given task is to learn from training data, and we use this measure to demonstrate that, when the teacher is perfect, assigning a large weight to the teacher's soft labels is advantageous. In the setting of an imperfect teacher, we show that hard labels serve to correct erroneous teacher predictions, thereby providing a theoretical justification for the common practice of combining hard and soft labels during training.

author: Gonzalez
title: Step-by-Step Guidance in Knowledge Distillation Through a Dual-Teacher Framework
abstract: Deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices is impeded by their substantial memory footprints and computational demands. Knowledge distillation addresses this by training a compact student network to absorb knowledge from a larger, pre-trained teacher model. Nevertheless, the majority of existing knowledge distillation approaches overlook the informative signals present throughout the training process itself, attending only to final training outcomes. We introduce the proposed method, a distillation strategy that coordinates two distinct teachers during student training. The first, a teacher trained from scratch, provides the student with intermediate, temporally evolving logits at each training step, steering the student along an optimal trajectory toward high-accuracy final predictions. The second, a pre-trained expert teacher, directs the student's attention toward task-critical regions in the feature space that are most discriminative for the target task. Combining the knowledge supplied by these two specialized teachers yields substantial gains in student network performance under knowledge distillation. Experiments conducted on the CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and Tiny ImageNet datasets confirm that the proposed method is computationally efficient and delivers state-of-the-art results.

author: Santos
title: Leveraging Channel-Wise Attention Mechanisms to Improve Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The goal of knowledge distillation is to compress the information a teacher network has learned from data into a student network, such that the student operates with fewer parameters and reduced computation while maintaining accuracy comparable to the teacher. We introduce a distillation framework comprising two distinct transfer strategies alongside a loss decay strategy. The first transfer strategy exploits channel-wise attention to convey channel-level information from the teacher to the student; we refer to this as Channel Distillation (CD). The second strategy, Guided Knowledge Distillation (GKD), departs from standard Knowledge Distillation (KD)—which trains the student to replicate the teacher's full per-sample prediction distribution—by restricting the student to imitate only those teacher outputs that are correct. The third component, Early Decay Teacher (EDT), progressively reduces the weight assigned to the distillation loss throughout training, with the objective of shifting optimization control from the teacher toward the student over time. The proposed method is assessed on ImageNet and CIFAR100. On ImageNet using ResNet18, a top-1 error of 27.68% is achieved, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods. On CIFAR100, the student attains an accuracy that exceeds that of the teacher, a notably surprising outcome. Code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhouzaida/channel-distillation.

author: Gardner
title: Transferring Adversarial Robustness Through Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Small neural networks obtained via knowledge distillation achieve strong classification performance, yet remain susceptible to adversarial attacks. We investigate the degree to which adversarial robustness is transferred from teacher to student during the distillation process. Our analysis reveals that students can inherit a substantial degree of robustness even when distillation is carried out exclusively on clean images. We then propose a method for robustness-aware distillation that, beyond replicating the high test accuracy of conventional distillation in compact models, additionally transfers the superior robustness of large teacher networks to the student. Experimentally, student models trained with the proposed method decisively outperform adversarially trained networks of identical architecture on robust accuracy metrics, exceeding state-of-the-art results on standard robustness benchmarks. We further demonstrate that recently proposed fast adversarial training techniques can be integrated into the proposed method to enable accelerated robust distillation.

author: Robinson
title: A Theoretical Framework for Ensemble Methods, Knowledge Distillation, and Self-Distillation in Deep Neural Networks
abstract: We present a formal analysis of why combining multiple deep learning models boosts test accuracy, and how knowledge distillation can compress this boost into a single model. Our setting is deliberately stringent: the ensemble is formed by averaging the outputs of several independently trained neural networks sharing the SAME architecture, the SAME training algorithm, and the SAME data set, with variation arising solely from the random seeds chosen at initialization. We demonstrate that the mechanisms underlying ensemble/knowledge distillation in deep learning differ fundamentally from those described by classical learning theory frameworks such as boosting or NTKs (neural tangent kernels). To account for these differences, we construct a theory in which data satisfying a property we call ``multi-view'' structure allows an ensemble of independently trained neural networks to achieve provably higher test accuracy; moreover, this higher test accuracy can be provably transferred into a single model by training it to match the ensemble's outputs rather than the ground-truth labels. Our findings illuminate the way ensemble operates in deep learning through a mechanism entirely distinct from what traditional theorems predict, and clarify how ``dark knowledge'' is encoded in the ensemble's outputs and made accessible during distillation. Finally, we establish that self-distillation can be interpreted as implicitly executing both ensemble and knowledge distillation in combination, yielding improved test accuracy.

author: Lawrence
title: Knowledge Distillation for Lightweight Visual Odometry via Deep Pose Regression
abstract: A novel approach is introduced for transferring knowledge from a deep pose regressor network to enable efficient Visual Odometry (VO). Conventional distillation methods depend on "dark knowledge" to facilitate effective knowledge transfer; however, pose regression tasks lack this information, and teacher predictions are not consistently reliable. To address this, the proposed method focuses knowledge transfer selectively on instances where the teacher is deemed trustworthy, accomplished by treating the teacher loss as a confidence score that assigns variable relative importance to teacher predictions. This confidence score is incorporated into the primary training objective through an attentive imitation loss formulation, as well as during learning of intermediate representations from the teacher via an attentive hint training strategy. To the best of our knowledge, no prior work has successfully demonstrated distillation from a deep pose regression network. Experiments conducted on the KITTI and Malaga datasets demonstrate that student predictions can be maintained close to teacher-level performance while achieving up to 92.95% reduction in parameters and a 2.12x improvement in computational speed.

author: Pacheco
title: Decision Boundary-Guided Knowledge Distillation via Adversarial Sample Exploitation
abstract: Although numerous studies have proposed techniques to transfer knowledge from a trained network to facilitate the learning of a new one, identifying an effective approach to knowledge distillation remains an unsolved challenge. We introduce a fresh viewpoint centered on the decision boundary, which constitutes one of the most critical elements of any classifier. Because the generalization capability of a classifier is tightly coupled with the appropriateness of its decision boundary, a well-performing classifier necessarily exhibits a well-formed decision boundary. Consequently, conveying information that is tightly linked to the decision boundary represents a promising direction for knowledge distillation. To achieve this, adversarial attacks are employed to locate samples that lie in close proximity to the decision boundary. Building on this principle, the proposed algorithm trains a student classifier by leveraging these adversarial samples that support the decision boundary, thereby transferring more precise information about it. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method yields meaningful improvements in knowledge distillation and attains state-of-the-art performance.

author: Smith
title: Quantifying the Knowledge Transferred in Distillation as a Means of Interpretation
abstract: A framework is introduced for interpreting why knowledge distillation succeeds by measuring and examining both task-relevant and task-irrelevant visual concepts encoded within intermediate layers of a deep neural network (DNN). To this end, three hypotheses are put forward: 1. Compared to learning from raw data, knowledge distillation causes the DNN to acquire a greater number of visual concepts. 2. Under knowledge distillation, the DNN tends to learn multiple visual concepts in parallel, whereas training directly on raw data leads the DNN to acquire visual concepts in a sequential manner. 3. The optimization directions produced by knowledge distillation are more stable than those observed when learning from raw data. To test these hypotheses, three categories of mathematical metrics are formulated to assess the feature representations learned by the DNN. Experimental evaluation across a range of DNNs confirms the validity of all three hypotheses.

author: Shaffer
title: Sample-Aware Knowledge Distillation for Improved Neural Machine Translation
abstract: Knowledge distillation has become a widely adopted technique in Neural Machine Translation (NMT) for boosting model performance by transferring teacher knowledge to a student model across training samples. Yet the varying influences of individual samples on this transfer process, and the relationships among them, have received little attention in prior work. We introduce an analytical protocol designed to systematically examine how different samples contribute to distillation by evaluating the effects of various sample partitions. Through extensive experiments guided by this protocol, we demonstrate that receiving more teacher knowledge is not unconditionally beneficial: knowledge transferred over certain samples can in fact degrade overall distillation performance. To remedy this, we propose two straightforward but effective selection strategies operating at the batch level and the global level, respectively, which identify samples that are well-suited for distillation. Our proposed method is evaluated on two large-scale translation benchmarks, WMT'14 English→German and WMT'19 Chinese→English, where it achieves gains of up to +1.28 and +0.89 BLEU points over the Transformer baseline, respectively.

author: Wolfe
title: Generative Pseudo Replay for Stable and Memory-Efficient Data-Free Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Knowledge transfer from a trained neural network (teacher) to a smaller one (student) without access to the original training data is the goal of Data-Free Knowledge Distillation (KD). Throughout the distillation process, prior works rely on a validation set to track student accuracy on real data and report the peak value observed at any point. Yet validation data may likewise be unavailable during distillation, rendering it impractical to retrieve the student snapshot corresponding to that peak accuracy. A practical data-free KD approach must therefore be robust and, ideally, yield student accuracy that increases monotonically over the course of distillation. Achieving this is difficult, as the student undergoes knowledge degradation caused by distribution shift in the synthetic data. One natural remedy is to periodically store and replay previously generated samples, but this inflates memory usage and raises privacy issues. The proposed method instead fits a generative network to the distribution of synthetic samples seen during distillation. Specifically, a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) is designed with a customized training objective that optimally captures representations of the synthetic data. Samples drawn from this VAE are then used in a generative pseudo replay scheme to rehearse the student, preventing knowledge degradation without retaining any samples in storage. On image classification benchmarks, the proposed method optimizes the expected accuracy of the distilled student model while avoiding the large memory overhead associated with sample-storing approaches.

author: Peterson
title: What Makes Knowledge Distillation Effective for Non-Autoregressive Machine Translation
abstract: Unlike autoregressive models, non-autoregressive machine translation (NAT) systems generate all output tokens simultaneously, yielding substantial gains in decoding speed. A standard ingredient in training NAT models is knowledge distillation, whereby training data is constructed from a pretrained autoregressive model to boost translation quality. Although knowledge distillation consistently produces large accuracy improvements in NAT, the underlying reasons for its effectiveness have remained poorly understood. Through carefully designed systematic experiments, we examine the mechanisms by which knowledge distillation benefits NAT training. Our analysis reveals two key findings: distillation reduces dataset complexity, and this reduction helps NAT models better capture the variability present in target outputs. We also observe a strong correlation between a given NAT model's capacity and the level of distilled data complexity that yields optimal translation quality. Building on these insights, we introduce several approaches that manipulate dataset complexity to further improve NAT performance. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results among NAT-based models and substantially narrows the gap relative to the autoregressive baseline on the WMT14 En-De benchmark.

author: Moore
title: Feature-Level Knowledge Distillation Through Attention-Guided Layer Matching
abstract: A pre-trained teacher network serves as the source of general knowledge in distillation, which is then transferred to guide the learning of a target student network. Intermediate features of the teacher and student are typically coupled through manually predefined links in the majority of existing work. Such manual selection frequently produces ineffective links, which constrain the gains achievable through distillation. Although prior work has attempted to tackle this issue, reliably identifying effective links under real-world practical scenarios remains difficult. We present a feature distillation approach that is both effective and efficient, leveraging all feature levels of the teacher while eliminating the need for manually chosen links. The proposed method employs an attention-based meta-network to capture relative similarities among features, and these learned similarities are then used to modulate distillation intensities across every possible teacher–student pair. Compared to the previous approach, the proposed method identifies competent links more efficiently and yields superior results on both model compression and transfer learning tasks. The contributions of the proposed method to improved distillation are further clarified through qualitative analyses and ablation studies. Code is publicly accessible at github.com/clovaai/attention-feature-distillation.

author: Bernard
title: Dynamic Teacher Weighting via Reinforcement Learning for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Pre-trained deep models present persistent deployment challenges in natural language processing (NLP) tasks, as their slow inference speed and substantial GPU memory requirements create bottlenecks for production use. Knowledge distillation, a widely adopted model compression technique, enables the transfer of knowledge from one or more large teacher models into a compact student model. Among existing multi-teacher distillation approaches, the predominant practice is to fix each teacher model's weight throughout the entire distillation process—and most methods go further by assigning an equal weight to every teacher. We find, however, that varying training example complexity and differing student model capacities mean that non-uniform, instance-level weighting of teacher models yields superior student model performance. To exploit this, we propose a reinforcement-based framework that dynamically determines per-instance weights for each teacher model, directly optimizing student model outcomes. Comprehensive experiments across multiple NLP tasks demonstrate that the proposed method is both feasible and effective.

author: Rogers
title: Multi-Teacher Knowledge Distillation Guided by Per-Sample Teacher Reliability
abstract: While knowledge distillation was originally designed to transfer supervision from a single teacher model to guide student model training, several recent approaches have sought to leverage richer and more varied knowledge by drawing on multiple teachers simultaneously. A common limitation of these existing methods is that they aggregate knowledge across teachers through simple averaging of logits or through other label-free combination strategies, both of which risk corrupting student learning when one or more teachers produce low-quality predictions. To address this shortcoming, the proposed method dynamically computes a per-sample reliability weight for every teacher prediction by consulting the ground-truth labels, assigning larger weights to those teacher predictions that lie closer to the corresponding one-hot labels. In addition, the proposed method integrates intermediate layers into the distillation pipeline to stabilize the overall knowledge transfer process. Through comprehensive experiments spanning a wide range of teacher-student architecture combinations, the proposed method is shown to consistently surpass all state-of-the-art baselines considered in the comparison.

author: Davis
title: Online Knowledge Distillation via Adversarial Feature-Map Transfer Across Networks
abstract: Image intensity and spatial correlation are richly encoded within feature maps, yet prior work on online knowledge distillation has been limited to leveraging class probabilities alone. To address this gap, we introduce an online distillation approach that simultaneously transfers knowledge from both class probabilities and feature maps by incorporating an adversarial training framework. Multiple networks are trained in parallel, with a dedicated discriminator assigned to each network; every discriminator is tasked with labeling its own network's feature maps as fake while treating those of the other networks as real. As a network learns to deceive its corresponding discriminator, it absorbs the feature map distribution of its peers. We demonstrate that this adversarial alignment outperforms conventional direct-matching objectives such as L1, and that it is better suited to the online distillation setting. Furthermore, a novel cyclic learning scheme is introduced to extend training beyond pairs to larger groups of networks. Experiments across multiple network architectures on image classification reveal substantial performance gains, with the most pronounced improvements observed when a small network and a large network are trained together as a pair.

author: Abbott
title: Adversarial Knowledge Distillation for Compressing Overparameterized Graph Neural Networks
abstract: While deep graph neural networks (GNNs) have demonstrated strong expressiveness in representing graph-structured data, their over-stacked architectures pose significant challenges for deployment and rapid inference on mobile or embedded platforms. Knowledge distillation through a teacher-student framework offers an effective path toward compressing such over-stacked GNNs, with the central challenge being the measurement of discrepancy between teacher and student networks using predefined distance functions. Yet applying a fixed distance metric across graphs of diverse structures is potentially ill-suited, and identifying the optimal distance formulation remains an open problem. To address this, the proposed method introduces an adversarial training approach in which a discriminator and a generator are jointly optimized to adaptively identify and reduce the teacher-student discrepancy. Given that inter-node and inter-class correlations are key to the effectiveness of deep GNNs, the proposed method evaluates the knowledge inherited by the student from both node-level and class-level perspectives using a trainable discriminator. While this discriminator learns to distinguish between teacher knowledge representations and those produced by the student, the student GNN acts as a generator whose objective is to deceive the discriminator. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed method is the first to bring adversarial training into knowledge distillation within graph domains. Evaluations on node-level and graph-level classification benchmarks show that the proposed method boosts student performance by a large margin, demonstrating its capacity to precisely transfer knowledge from a complex teacher GNN into a compact student GNN.

author: Munoz
title: Knowledge Distillation from Deep Networks Without Any Training Data
abstract: Training a compact Student model to approximate the performance of a high-capacity Teacher model is the central objective of knowledge distillation. Prior work in this area relies on the original training data or on meta-data derived from it to carry out Student training. Yet, access to the dataset used to train the Teacher is not always possible—whether because of its scale, or because it contains sensitive information such as biometric or medical records that raise privacy or safety concerns. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that requires no data whatsoever to transfer knowledge from Teacher to Student. Rather than relying on any meta-data, synthetic samples—referred to here as Data Impressions—are generated directly from the Teacher model and used as stand-ins for the original training examples, enabling knowledge distillation without any real data. We call this proposed method "Zero-Shot Knowledge Distillation" and show, across several benchmark datasets, that it achieves generalization performance competitive with distillation carried out using the actual training samples.

author: Roman
title: Bias Mitigation Through Feature Distillation for Vision-Based Recognition
abstract: In computer vision, and particularly in systems that make human-related decisions, fairness has emerged as a matter of growing importance. Yet ensuring algorithmic fairness—whereby a model yields non-discriminatory outputs with respect to protected groups—remains an open challenge. We introduce a principled framework that addresses algorithmic biases through feature distillation applied to visual recognition, referred to hereafter as the proposed method. Although distillation techniques have been broadly adopted to enhance prediction accuracy, to the best of our knowledge no prior work has explicitly leveraged distillation as a mechanism for improving fairness as well. In addition, we provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed method that characterizes the joint effects of knowledge distillation on both fairness and model performance. Across a wide range of experiments conducted on synthetic and real-world face datasets, the proposed method is shown to substantially reduce bias against specific minority groups while incurring no loss in accuracy.

author: Blair
title: A Rigorous Examination of Policy Distillation Methods and Their Variants
abstract: In Deep Reinforcement Learning, transferring knowledge between policies is a valuable technique. Known as distillation, this approach has yielded considerable success — for instance, by improving agent optimisation to achieve stronger performance more rapidly on challenging domains [26, 32, 5, 8]. Although distillation is both conceptually straightforward and widely adopted, the numerous formulations encountered in practice differ in subtle ways that can produce dramatic changes in performance and in the underlying objective being optimised. We systematically examine the full space of policy distillation through both theoretical and empirical lenses, analysing the motivations and relative strengths of each variant. Three distillation techniques emerge from our results as preferable, with the choice among them depending on the specifics of the task at hand. In particular, a newly proposed distillation formulation incorporating expected entropy regularisation enables faster learning across a broad set of situations while still providing convergence guarantees.

author: Herrera
title: Fine-grained Feature Imitation for Knowledge Distillation in Object Detection
abstract: Deploying high-performing CNN-based recognition models on resource-constrained devices is frequently impractical due to their computational demands. Knowledge distillation offers a compelling general strategy to overcome this barrier, training a compact student model to replicate the outputs of a heavy teacher model in order to achieve better generalization. Nevertheless, existing distillation approaches are predominantly designed for classification and overlook more complex tasks such as object detection. We demonstrate that directly applying vanilla knowledge distillation to detection models yields only marginal improvement. To address this gap, we introduce a fine-grained feature imitation approach that leverages the cross-location discrepancy in feature response across the spatial extent of feature maps. The underlying intuition is that detectors are primarily sensitive to local regions in the vicinity of objects, meaning that differences in feature response at anchor locations near objects carry particularly informative signals about how the teacher model generalizes. We develop a novel mechanism to identify these locations and guide the student model to imitate the teacher specifically at those positions, thereby boosting performance. Initial validation is conducted on a lightweight toy detector embodying the core principles of modern anchor-based detection models on the challenging KITTI dataset, where the proposed method delivers up to 15% mAP improvement for the student model relative to the non-imitated baseline. Extensive experiments are then carried out using the Faster R-CNN architecture across diverse settings on the Pascal VOC and COCO benchmarks, where imitation reduces the student model's performance gap with the teacher by up to 74%. Code is available at https://github.com/twangnh/Distilling-Object-Detectors

author: Dudley
title: Answer Span Distillation with Alignment Guidance for Reading Comprehension
abstract: Current reading comprehension systems typically rely on ensembling many models to achieve strong results, and they remain susceptible to adversarial attacks. To address both issues, this work exploits knowledge distillation as a mechanism for transferring what an ensemble model has learned into a single model. We begin by showing that applying vanilla knowledge distillation to answer span prediction already yields meaningful gains for reading comprehension. Building on this, the proposed method introduces two new techniques that jointly discourage incorrect predictions on confusing answers and incorporate alignment information distilled from the ensemble as a training signal. On the SQuAD test set, the best student model trails the ensemble teacher by only 0.4% F1 while achieving 12x faster inference. Notably, the student surpasses the teacher on both adversarial SQuAD datasets and the NarrativeQA benchmark.

author: Gray
title: Compressing BERT Through Iterative Module Substitution
abstract: We present a novel model compression method that achieves effective compression of BERT via progressive module substitution. The original BERT is first partitioned into a set of modules, each paired with a compact replacement. During training, these compact replacements are inserted in place of the original modules at random, so that the replacements learn to replicate the behavior of the original modules. A key aspect of the proposed method is that the probability of substitution is gradually raised over the course of training, enabling a deeper level of interaction between the original and compact models than prior work achieves. Unlike existing knowledge distillation approaches to BERT compression, no additional loss function of any kind is introduced by the proposed method. Evaluation on the GLUE benchmark demonstrates that the proposed method surpasses existing knowledge distillation approaches, offering a new perspective on model compression.

author: Arnold
title: Knowledge Distillation: An Examination of Whether It Functions as Theorized
abstract: Training a compact student network to mimic a larger teacher model — such as a network ensemble — is a widely used application of knowledge distillation. We demonstrate that, although knowledge distillation is capable of enhancing student generalization, it frequently fails to operate in the manner conventionally assumed: the predictive distributions of the teacher and student often diverge by a surprisingly wide margin, even in settings where the student possesses sufficient capacity to replicate the teacher exactly. We establish that optimization difficulties are a primary factor preventing the student from matching the teacher's predictive distributions. Furthermore, we show that the composition of the dataset employed during distillation influences how closely the student replicates the teacher — and that, paradoxically, a closer match to the teacher does not consistently translate into improved student generalization.

author: Calderon
title: Knowledge Distillation for Cross-Distribution Generalization in Neural Vehicle Routing Solvers
abstract: Existing neural approaches to vehicle routing problems typically train and evaluate deep models under identical instance distributions (i.e., uniform), leaving cross-distribution generalization as an open challenge. To address this limitation, we introduce knowledge distillation into this domain and develop a proposed method — an adaptive scheme that distills knowledge from multiple distributions to produce more generalizable deep models. Specifically, the proposed method draws on diverse knowledge from several teachers, each trained on a distinct exemplar distribution, in order to train a light-weight yet generalist student model. An adaptive strategy is further incorporated, enabling the student to allocate greater attention to distributions it finds difficult and thereby more effectively absorb hard-to-master knowledge. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive performance relative to baseline neural methods on both unseen in-distribution and out-of-distribution instances — whether randomly synthesized or drawn from established benchmark datasets (i.e., TSPLIB and CVRPLIB). Furthermore, the proposed method is generic in design and demands fewer computational resources at inference time.

author: Montgomery
title: Dynamic Graph-Based 3D Object Detection via Message Passing on Point Clouds
abstract: Existing pipelines for 3D object detection are often complex at both training and inference stages, demanding deep domain-specific knowledge for each individual dataset. Drawing motivation from recent 2D detection models that operate without non-maximum suppression, we introduce an architecture for detecting 3D objects directly from point clouds. The proposed method frames 3D object detection as a message passing problem over a dynamic graph, extending the DGCNN framework to produce a set-valued prediction of objects. Within this design, object confidence aggregation and non-maximum suppression are both eliminated from post-processing. We additionally introduce a set-to-set distillation strategy tailored specifically to the 3D detection setting, which aligns teacher model and student model outputs in a permutation-invariant manner, thereby substantially reducing the complexity of knowledge distillation for this task. On autonomous driving benchmarks, the proposed method reaches state-of-the-art performance. Extensive analysis of both the detection architecture and the distillation framework is also presented.

author: Hensley
title: Leveraging Knowledge Distillation to Enhance Accuracy in Low-Precision Neural Networks
abstract: On computer vision tasks such as image classification and object detection, state-of-the-art accuracies are routinely delivered by deep learning networks. These top-performing systems, however, tend to rely on large models with vast numbers of parameters. Such high-accuracy models—frequently deep, wide, or both—present a significant deployment challenge on inference hardware with limited resources, owing to their heavy compute and memory demands. Two widely adopted strategies for reducing the memory footprint and computational cost of deployed models are low-precision numerics and model compression via knowledge distillation. We investigate the joint application of these two strategies and demonstrate that knowledge distillation techniques can yield substantial accuracy gains in low-precision networks. Evaluated on the ImageNet dataset using variants of the ResNet architecture, the proposed method attains state-of-the-art accuracies at both ternary precision and 4-bit precision. Three distinct schemes are introduced through which knowledge distillation can be integrated at different stages of the train-and-deploy pipeline.

author: Ray
title: Knowledge Distillation as a Vehicle for Propagating Inductive Biases Across Models
abstract: In many settings where compute or data are constrained, or where a gap exists between training conditions and test-time conditions, having appropriate inductive biases can be decisive. Yet specifying, constructing, and effectively tuning inductive biases is far from trivial. We investigate knowledge distillation as a mechanism for conveying the influence of inductive biases from a teacher model to a student model. Model families with contrasting inductive biases—LSTMs versus Transformers and CNNs versus MLPs—are examined across tasks and scenarios in which correct inductive biases are critical to success. Beyond measuring performance alone, we analyze what effect inductive biases have on the solutions models arrive at, and probe how, and to what degree, that effect is propagated to the student through knowledge distillation, encompassing multiple dimensions of the converged solutions.

author: Bush
title: Boosting Multi-Label Image Classification Through Knowledge Distillation from a Weakly-Supervised Detection Teacher
abstract: Towards general visual understanding, multi-label image classification represents a core yet difficult problem. Prior work has demonstrated that region-level cues, such as features extracted from RoIs, are beneficial for multi-label classification. However, these approaches typically depend on costly object-level annotations—including bounding boxes and object labels—to learn object-level visual features effectively. We introduce an efficient and novel deep framework in which a weakly-supervised detection task transfers knowledge to improve multi-label classification, entirely without bounding box annotations. Using only image-level annotations, the proposed method proceeds in two steps: (1) a weakly-supervised detection (WSD) model is trained, and (2) a multi-label image classification model is built within an end-to-end framework incorporating a knowledge distillation module. This module uses the WSD model to supervise the classification model through both class-level predictions over the full image and object-level visual features corresponding to object RoIs. In this setup, the WSD model acts as the teacher model while the classification model serves as the student model. Because the WSD model can be discarded entirely at test time, the efficiency of the student model is preserved after cross-task knowledge distillation, while its performance is substantially enhanced. Evaluated on two large-scale benchmarks, MS-COCO and NUS-WIDE, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches across both accuracy and efficiency metrics.

author: Williams
title: Relation-Centered Knowledge Distillation for Graph-Free Link Prediction
abstract: Link prediction is a task in which Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated outstanding effectiveness. However, the substantial inference latency stemming from their inherent neighborhood data dependency makes GNNs difficult to deploy in real-world systems. MLPs, while computationally efficient, fall considerably short of GNNs in this task because they lack access to relational knowledge. To capture the strengths of both architectures, we first investigate straightforward knowledge distillation (KD) approaches adapted for link prediction, namely matching on predicted logits and on node representations. Finding that these direct KD analogs are insufficient for link prediction, we introduce a relational KD framework—the proposed method—that transfers relational knowledge to a student MLP for the purpose of link prediction. Whereas simple KD techniques operate on independent link logits or isolated node representations, the proposed method instead distills relational knowledge organized around each anchor node and delivers it to the student MLP. To achieve this, we develop two complementary strategies: rank-based matching and distribution-based matching. Through extensive experiments, we show that the proposed method substantially improves MLP link prediction performance, even surpassing the teacher GNNs on 7 of 8 benchmarks. On the large-scale OGB dataset, the proposed method further achieves a 70.68x reduction in link prediction inference time relative to GNNs.

author: Perez
title: Black-Box Unsupervised Domain Adaptation from One or Several Source Predictors
abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) reduces the cost of annotation by leveraging knowledge from previously labeled datasets (sources) to improve performance on a new unlabeled dataset (target). Although existing methods have achieved strong results, they typically require direct access to the raw source data and rely on data-dependent alignment strategies to classify target samples in a transductive learning setting, which can compromise the privacy of source individuals. Some recent works address this by using a white-box model trained on the source domain instead of the raw data, but such models can still expose the original source data via generative adversarial learning. We investigate a practical UDA scenario in which only black-box source models are available during target-domain adaptation—that is, only the network predictions can be queried. Our solution is a two-step knowledge adaptation framework in which the proposed method first distills knowledge from the source predictor into a customized target model designed to reflect the structure of the target data, and then fine-tunes the distilled model to better fit the target domain. Furthermore, the proposed method does not require the neural networks across domains to share the same architecture, which enables effective adaptation even on low-resource devices. Experiments across three UDA scenarios—single-source, multi-source, and partial-set—demonstrate that the proposed method achieves highly competitive performance relative to state-of-the-art data-dependent approaches. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tim-learn/DINE/}.

author: Roberts
title: Enhancing Decision Tree Interpretability in Deep Neural Networks via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: From speech recognition and computer vision to language modeling, Deep Neural Networks have demonstrated remarkable success across a broad range of tasks. Yet strong performance alone is increasingly insufficient for real-world deployment: interpretability is a firm requirement in mission critical and ethics-sensitive contexts. Because Deep Neural Networks are inherently complex, reasoning about and understanding their predictions remains difficult, impeding further adoption. To address this challenge, we leverage the Knowledge Distillation technique to transfer Deep Neural Networks into decision trees, simultaneously achieving competitive performance and interpretability. The distillation is cast as a multi-output regression problem, and our experiments show that the student model attains substantially higher accuracy (approximately 1% to 5%) relative to vanilla decision trees operating at an equivalent tree depth. All experiments are conducted on the TensorFlow platform to ensure scalability to large datasets. To the best of our knowledge, distilling Deep Neural Networks into vanilla decision trees on multi-class datasets has not been previously explored.

author: Miller
title: Analyzing Knowledge Distillation for BERT-Based Ranking Models
abstract: Large-scale pre-training on extensive corpora has enabled deep language models like BERT to substantially advance state-of-the-art ranking performance in information retrieval systems. The rich knowledge encoded in these models equips them to capture intricate relevance signals between queries and passages. Nevertheless, the considerable computational overhead at inference time poses a significant barrier to deploying such models in practical search applications. We investigate whether and in what manner search-oriented knowledge within BERT can be transferred via distillation into a more compact ranker. Our experimental results show that selecting an appropriate distillation procedure is critical, with the proposed method achieving up to nine times speedup without sacrificing state-of-the-art ranking effectiveness.

author: Hall
title: Zero-Shot Distillation for Federated Learning Across Heterogeneous On-Device Models Under Resource Constraints
abstract: Without centralizing local data, federated learning allows geographically distributed devices to jointly train a shared prediction model. A fundamental limitation of most existing algorithms is their requirement that all participants use on-device models of identical structure and size for local training, which effectively excludes resource-constrained devices from participation. To address the heterogeneity of real-world device ecosystems, we introduce a federated learning framework in which each device is free to adopt on-device models suited to its own local resources. Knowledge transfer across these heterogeneous on-device models is achieved through a zero-shot distillation procedure that, in contrast to prior approaches relying on a public dataset or a pre-trained data generator, requires no access whatsoever to private on-device data. The computationally demanding distillation process is handled entirely by the server rather than the devices, enabling resource-constrained participants to take part: the server adversarially trains a generator using the ensemble of on-device models it has collected. The central knowledge produced through distillation is delivered back to each device in the form of updated parameters for its corresponding on-device model, which can be readily incorporated on the device side. Through extensive experiments, the proposed method demonstrates both effectiveness and robustness under conditions including on-device knowledge agnosticism, on-device model heterogeneity, and other challenging federated learning settings such as heterogeneous on-device data distributions and straggler effects.

author: Garcia
title: Knowledge Distillation for Compression of Visual-Linguistic Transformer Models
abstract: While substantial advances have been made in pre-training visual-linguistic (VL) representations, efforts toward compact VL models remain scarce. We investigate knowledge distillation (KD) as a mechanism to compress a large transformer-based VL model into a small VL model. A core difficulty stems from the fact that regional visual tokens produced by the Teacher's and Student's detectors are inconsistent, causing misalignment in both hidden representations and attention distributions. Our proposed method resolves this by retraining and adapting the Teacher using region proposals drawn from the Student's detector, while retaining features from the Teacher's own object detector. This alignment of network inputs enables the adapted Teacher to transfer knowledge through intermediate representations effectively. To accomplish this, mean square error loss is applied to replicate attention distributions within transformer blocks, and a token-wise noise contrastive loss is introduced to align hidden states by contrasting them against negative representations held in a sample queue. The proposed distillation yields substantial gains for small VL models on visual question answering and image captioning benchmarks. On COCO captioning, a CIDEr score of 120.8 is achieved—5.1 points above the non-distilled counterpart—while on VQA 2.0, an accuracy of 69.8 is obtained, reflecting a 0.8 improvement over the baseline. Comprehensive ablations and experiments validate the effectiveness of VL distillation across both fine-tuning and pre-training stages.

author: Ramirez
title: Iterative Target Smoothing via a Model's Own Predictions for Self-Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Numerous regularization strategies—including constraining the function space, introducing stochasticity at training time, and performing data augmentation—have led to substantial gains in the generalization of deep neural networks. We introduce a straightforward yet powerful regularization approach in which a model's own predictions are progressively used to soften hard targets (i.e., one-hot vectors) throughout training, a process interpretable under the knowledge distillation framework as one in which the student itself assumes the role of teacher. In the proposed method, targets are adaptively constructed by blending ground-truth labels with the model's own predictions from previous training stages. We demonstrate that the proposed method implicitly performs hard example mining by rescaling gradients in proportion to the classification difficulty of each example. It is broadly applicable to any supervised learning scenario that relies on hard targets and integrates seamlessly with existing regularization techniques to yield additional generalization gains. Beyond accuracy, the proposed method is shown to improve confidence estimate quality, measured both by calibration and ordinal ranking. Through extensive experiments spanning image classification, object detection, and machine translation, we confirm that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across all three tasks. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/lgcnsai/PS-KD-Pytorch.

author: Reid
title: Structural Distillation for Memory Efficiency via Simple Convolutional Transformations
abstract: The deployment of contemporary neural networks in resource-constrained, memory-limited environments is a common goal among practitioners, yet principled approaches to memory reduction remain underdeveloped, and the associated accuracy trade-offs are poorly understood. We introduce a structural model distillation approach in which the student architecture is derived from the teacher architecture through a straightforward transformation, requiring neither manual redesign nor adjustment of hyperparameters. Leveraging attention transfer, the proposed method generates Pareto curves and tables characterizing the memory–accuracy trade-off for distillation of residual networks across four benchmark datasets. Our results demonstrate that large reductions in memory are attainable at only a marginal accuracy cost, and further confirm that a student network trained via distillation consistently outperforms the same student architecture trained directly on the data.

author: Diaz
title: Two-stage Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Teachers for Compressing Web Question Answering Models
abstract: Question answering has seen remarkable advances through deep pre-training and fine-tuning approaches such as BERT and OpenAI GPT; however, the enormous number of parameters in these models results in very slow inference, making their deployment in real-world business settings a challenging yet important problem. Existing model compression techniques typically incur information loss throughout the compression process, yielding models that perform worse than the original. To address this, the proposed method introduces a two-stage distillation pipeline that draws on multiple teacher models for web question answering. In the first stage, a general question-and-answer distillation task is used to pre-train the student model; in the second stage, this pre-trained student model is fine-tuned on downstream tasks—including a Web Q&A task along with MNLI, SNLI, and RTE tasks from GLUE—using multi-teacher knowledge distillation, which mitigates overfitting bias present in any single teacher and enables more general knowledge to be transferred to the student model. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method substantially surpasses baseline compression methods and even attains performance comparable to the original teacher models, while delivering considerable speedup in model inference.

author: Wood
title: Toward a Statistical Understanding of Data Augmentation in Knowledge Distillation: What Constitutes an Effective Choice?
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly applicable neural network training paradigm in which a student model is trained under the supervision of a teacher model. While the bulk of prior research has approached KD from the perspective of the network output—focusing, for instance, on improving the KD loss function—comparatively little attention has been paid to the input side of the pipeline. In particular, how data augmentation (DA) interacts with KD remains poorly understood. We address the following questions: Why do certain DA strategies (e.g., CutMix) consistently outperform others within the KD framework? What properties define a "good" DA for KD? Analyzing this problem through a statistical lens, we find that an effective DA scheme is one that lowers the covariance of the teacher-student cross-entropy. We further derive a practical diagnostic metric—the standard deviation of the teacher's mean probability (T. stddev)—and provide thorough empirical justification for its use. Beyond theoretical insight, the proposed method introduces CutMixPick, a novel entropy-guided data-mixing DA strategy designed to improve upon CutMix. Comprehensive experiments validate our theoretical claims and show that substantial performance improvements in knowledge distillation can be achieved simply by selecting a more suitable DA scheme.

author: Clark
title: Ultra-Resolution Universal Style Transfer via Encoder-Decoder Collaborative Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Deep CNN models such as VGG-19, pre-trained on large image collections, supply the rich representations that universal style transfer methods typically depend on. However, the large model size required by these approaches severely limits their ability to process ultra-resolution images under memory constraints. We introduce a knowledge distillation approach for encoder-decoder based neural style transfer that reduces convolutional filters by exploiting a newly identified phenomenon: encoder-decoder pairs form an exclusive collaborative relationship, which we treat as a novel category of knowledge specific to style transfer models. To address feature size mismatch that arises during the distillation process, we additionally propose a linear embedding loss that guides the student network toward learning a linear embedding of the teacher's features. Through extensive experiments across multiple universal style transfer frameworks—WCT and AdaIN—the proposed method demonstrates consistent effectiveness even when model size is compressed by a factor of 15.5. Notably, applying the proposed method to WCT with compressed models enables ultra-resolution (exceeding 40 megapixels) universal style transfer on a 12GB GPU, achieved here for the first time. Additional experiments conducted under an optimization-based stylization scheme confirm that the proposed method generalizes across different stylization paradigms. Code and trained models are publicly available at https://github.com/mingsun-tse/collaborative-distillation.

author: Adams
title: Revisiting Deep Learning Training Heuristics: An Empirical Study of Distillation, Warmup, and Learning Rate Restarts
abstract: Heuristics such as learning rate schedules, skip connections, normalization layers, and knowledge distillation have yielded substantial gains in both convergence rate and final performance for widely used deep learning models. Because theoretical foundations for these strategies remain largely absent, controlled experiments designed to illuminate their behavior can deepen our understanding of training dynamics and loss landscapes. Prior empirical analyses have depended on linear interpolation and dimensionality-reduction-based visualizations, each carrying notable limitations. We instead examine these heuristics through two recently introduced analytical lenses—mode connectivity and canonical correlation analysis (CCA)—and use them to put forward hypotheses about why these strategies succeed. Specifically, knowledge distillation together with the learning rate heuristics of (cosine) restarts and warmup are investigated via mode connectivity and CCA. The findings of our empirical study indicate that: (a) the explanations commonly cited for the effectiveness of cosine annealing are not supported by experimental evidence; (b) learning rate warmup functions primarily by preventing deeper layers from inducing instability during training; and (c) the latent knowledge conveyed by the teacher is distributed predominantly to the deeper layers of the student.

author: Zuniga
title: Online distillation for large-scale distributed training of neural networks
abstract: Methods like distillation and ensembling can improve the quality of nearly any base model, yet both carry practical drawbacks—ensembling raises cost at inference time, while distillation introduces a complicated multi-stage training pipeline—that make them difficult to deploy in production environments. We investigate a distillation variant that sidesteps these issues by requiring neither a cumbersome multi-stage setup nor a large number of new hyperparameters. Our first claim is that, by exploiting additional parallelism, online distillation allows very large datasets to be trained on roughly twice as fast. Importantly, this speedup remains achievable even at the point where adding more parallelism no longer benefits synchronous or asynchronous stochastic gradient descent. When two neural networks are each trained on a separate, disjoint partition of the data, knowledge can be transferred between them by penalizing disagreement with the predictions the other network would produce. Because these predictions may be drawn from a stale snapshot of the other model, they can be computed safely from weights that are only infrequently communicated. Our second claim is that online distillation provides a cost-effective mechanism for making the deterministic predictions of a model substantially more reproducible. We validate both claims through experiments on ImageNet, the Criteo Display Ad Challenge dataset, and the largest dataset employed to date for neural language modeling—a corpus of $6\times 10^{11}$ tokens derived from the Common Crawl web data repository.

author: Wong
title: Leveraging Soft Targets from Teacher Networks: A Knowledge Distillation Approach to Domain Generalization via Gradient Regularization
abstract: A persistent obstacle to the practical deployment of convolutional neural networks is their limited generalization capability when training data are insufficient or unrepresentative. We introduce a plug-and-play, straightforward, and effective training strategy built upon a knowledge distillation framework that incorporates a gradient filter as a novel regularization term. Our analysis reveals that the richer dark knowledge produced by the teacher network, together with the proposed gradient filter, jointly reduce the difficulty of learning the underlying mapping and thereby strengthen the generalization ability of the resulting model. Through extensive experiments spanning image classification, segmentation, and reinforcement learning, the proposed method is shown to substantially outperform existing state-of-the-art domain generalization techniques in improving the generalization capability of deep neural networks. Furthermore, two diagnostic metrics are proposed to analyze the proposed method, offering deeper insight into the mechanisms through which it enhances the generalization capability of deep neural networks.

author: Lynch
title: Knowledge Distillation Through the Lens of Label Smoothing: A Reexamination
abstract: A lightweight student model can acquire compressed knowledge from a heavy teacher model through Knowledge Distillation (KD), whose effectiveness is widely believed to stem from the teacher's ability to convey inter-class similarity information encoded in its outputs—an assumption that restricts practical deployment to cases where the teacher outperforms the student. We contest this prevailing view on the basis of two experimental findings: 1) not only does the teacher boost student performance, but reversing the KD procedure allows the student to substantially improve the teacher as well; 2) a teacher trained poorly enough to achieve far lower accuracy than the student can nonetheless yield meaningful gains for that student. To account for these findings, we develop a theoretical framework characterizing the connection between KD and label smoothing regularization, demonstrating that 1) KD constitutes a form of learned label smoothing regularization, and 2) label smoothing regularization implicitly defines a virtual teacher for use in KD. These results lead us to conclude that soft-target regularization contributes to KD's success at least as much as—if not more than—inter-category similarity information supplied by the teacher. Building on this analysis, we introduce a framework in which no external teacher is required: the student trains against its own predictions or a hand-crafted regularization distribution. This proposed method attains performance on par with standard KD using a superior teacher, making it valuable when no stronger teacher is available. The proposed method is also broadly applicable and can be incorporated directly into deep neural network training pipelines. With no additional computational overhead, it yields accuracy gains of up to 0.65% on ImageNet relative to well-established baselines, surpassing conventional label smoothing regularization.

author: Jackson
title: Mutual Contrastive Learning for Teacher-Free Online Knowledge Distillation in Visual Recognition
abstract: Teacher-free online Knowledge Distillation (KD) involves collaboratively training multiple student models that distill knowledge from one another. While existing online KD approaches deliver competitive results, they predominantly treat class probabilities as the principal knowledge type, overlooking the rich information contained in feature representations. We introduce a framework based on mutual contrastive learning for online KD. The central principle of the proposed method is to enable networks within a cohort to mutually exchange and transfer contrastive distributions in an online fashion. By aggregating embedding information across networks and maximizing a lower bound on the mutual information shared between any two networks, the proposed method allows each network to acquire additional contrastive knowledge from its peers. This results in improved feature representations and, consequently, stronger performance on visual recognition tasks. The proposed method is further extended beyond the final layer to intermediate layers, where an adaptive layer-matching mechanism optimized via meta-optimization is applied. Evaluated on image classification and transfer learning benchmarks for visual recognition, the layer-wise formulation of the proposed method yields consistent improvements over state-of-the-art online KD methods. These gains confirm that guiding networks through layer-wise mutual contrastive learning produces higher-quality feature representations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/winycg/L-MCL.

author: Daniel
title: Adversarial Knowledge Distillation Without Training Data
abstract: Over recent years, Knowledge Distillation (KD) has emerged as a widely adopted approach for model compression and knowledge transfer, achieving substantial advances. Nevertheless, virtually every existing KD technique is data-driven — that is, it depends on large quantities of the original training data or some substitute data, neither of which tends to be accessible in practical deployment settings. This paper addresses that difficult scenario by introducing an adversarial distillation mechanism capable of producing a compact student model in the complete absence of real-world data. A model discrepancy metric is defined to quantitatively capture the divergence between the student and teacher, and a tractable optimizable upper bound on this quantity is constructed. The student and the teacher together serve as a discriminator working to minimize this discrepancy, while a generator adversarially synthesizes "hard samples" with the opposing objective of maximizing it. Through extensive experiments, the proposed data-free approach is shown to achieve performance comparable to existing data-driven KD methods. Most notably, the method generalizes directly to semantic segmentation — a task considerably more complex than classification — where it attains state-of-the-art results. Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/VainF/Data-Free-Adversarial-Distillation.

author: Martin
title: BERT Knowledge Distillation for Attention-Based Sequence-to-Sequence Speech Recognition
abstract: Although attention-based seq2seq models have shown strong performance in automatic speech recognition (ASR), their left-to-right decoding mechanism prevents them from utilizing right-side context. The proposed method addresses this limitation by incorporating BERT as an external language model via knowledge distillation, enabling the seq2seq ASR model to benefit from both left and right context. Specifically, BERT is used to produce soft labels that supervise seq2seq ASR training. In addition, the proposed method supplies BERT with context drawn from outside the current utterance. On the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese (CSJ), experiments demonstrate that the proposed method yields substantial gains over the seq2seq baseline. Distilling knowledge from BERT proves more effective than distilling from a transformer LM restricted to left context. The utility of incorporating cross-utterance context is also demonstrated. Compared with alternative language model integration strategies such as shallow fusion and n-best rescoring, the proposed method achieves superior ASR performance without incurring any additional inference cost.

author: Gray
title: Boosting Feature Distillation Through an Ensemble of Projectors
abstract: While prior work on feature distillation has largely concentrated on crafting loss functions and choosing which layers to distill, the role of the feature projector situated between the student and the teacher has received comparatively little attention.
