This paper begins by offering a plausible explanation of how the projector functions, supported by empirical evidence, and then introduces a new feature distillation approach built around a projector ensemble to achieve further performance improvement. A key observation is that the student network gains from having a projector even when the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are identical. When a student backbone is trained without a projector, the optimization can be viewed as a multi-task learning problem: the network must simultaneously learn discriminative feature extraction for classification and perform feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation. We hypothesize—and empirically confirm—that the absence of a projector causes the student network to overfit the teacher's feature distributions in spite of architectural differences and distinct weight initializations. This overfitting degrades the quality of the deep features the student ultimately relies on for classification. Introducing a projector, by contrast, decouples these two objectives, allowing the student network to concentrate more effectively on the primary feature extraction task while still leveraging teacher features as a supervisory signal through the projector. Building on the demonstrated benefit of the projector in feature distillation, the proposed method extends this by employing an ensemble of projectors to further improve student feature quality. Evaluations conducted across multiple datasets using a range of teacher-student pairs demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

author: Mayo
title: Soft Labels in Knowledge Distillation Through the Lens of Bias-Variance Tradeoff
abstract: A well-trained network, or an ensemble thereof, can serve as a teacher to supervise the training of a student network—a paradigm known as knowledge distillation. In this framework, the teacher's predictions function as soft labels that guide student training. Prior work has highlighted a noteworthy characteristic of such soft labels: label smoothing via teacher outputs acts as an effective regularizer for the student. While regularization is classically understood to reduce variance in statistical learning, precisely how bias and variance each evolve under soft-label training remains an open question. We address this gap by systematically analyzing the bias-variance tradeoff induced when distillation is performed with soft labels. Our analysis reveals that this tradeoff manifests differently across individual training samples. Furthermore, at any fixed distillation temperature, distillation quality degrades as the proportion of a particular category of samples grows—those that simultaneously increase bias and decrease variance, which we refer to as regularization samples. Counterintuitively, however, our empirical results also show that entirely removing regularization samples from training is itself harmful to distillation performance. Motivated by these findings, the proposed method introduces a sample-adaptive weighting scheme over soft labels, enabling the student network to manage the per-sample bias-variance tradeoff dynamically. Validation across standard benchmarks confirms the effectiveness of this approach. Code is available at https://github.com/bellymonster/Weighted-Soft-Label-Distillation.

author: Bowman
title: Compact Distilled Speech Models for Universal Paralinguistic Representation
abstract: Self-supervised learning has recently led to substantial gains in the quality of speech representations, yet on-device deployment of leading embedding models remains constrained by their large resource footprint and limited public availability. We address both problems by openly releasing a suite of paralinguistic speech models that are compact while retaining near state-of-the-art performance. The proposed method relies on knowledge distillation, and distillation is carried out exclusively on publicly available data. We investigate multiple architectures and conduct thorough evaluation on the Non-Semantic Speech (NOSS) benchmark. Compared with the original model (2.2GB), our largest distilled model occupies less than 15% of that storage (314MB), is trained on only 6.5% of the data, and surpasses 96% of the original accuracy on 6 out of 7 tasks. Our most compact model, at just 22MB (1% of the original size), still exceeds 90% of the original accuracy on 6 of 7 tasks. Across 6 of 7 tasks the proposed models surpass the open-source Wav2Vec 2.0 baseline, and even our smallest model outperforms the open-source Wav2Vec 2.0 on both emotion recognition tasks, despite being only 7% of its size.

author: Hawkins
title: Efficient Knowledge Distillation for Image Recognition via Soft Label Generation
abstract: Knowledge Distillation (KD) has proven valuable across numerous visual tasks, including supervised classification and self-supervised representation learning. Nevertheless, the central limitation of a vanilla KD pipeline is that most of the computational cost is spent on forward passes through large teacher networks, rendering the overall training procedure slow and resource-intensive. A recently introduced approach, ReLabel, addresses this by constructing a label map over the full image and retrieving region-level supervision through RoI align operations on that pre-computed map, thereby avoiding repeated teacher inference. Yet, because the teacher networks in this scheme follow conventional multi-crop training, substantial mismatches arise between the global label map and the corresponding region-level labels, leading to degraded performance. We introduce the proposed method, a distillation framework that faithfully reproduces the multi-crop KD training process and produces soft labels accordingly, while achieving greater training speed than ReLabel by eliminating post-processing steps such as RoI align and softmax computation. When multi-crop sampling is performed within a single image during data loading, the proposed method proves even more computationally efficient than a standard image classification pipeline. On ImageNet-1K, the proposed method achieves 79.8% top-1 accuracy with ResNet-50, surpassing ReLabel by approximately 1.0% while running faster. Efficiency benefits of the proposed method are further demonstrated on self-supervised learning tasks. Source code, pretrained models, and additional details are publicly available.

author: Cohen
title: Attention-Driven Fusion of Teacher Layers for Improved Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Two neural networks—referred to as a teacher and a student—are jointly trained under the knowledge distillation paradigm, which simultaneously serves as a compression strategy and a training methodology. While the teacher acts as a reliable predictor, the student is trained to replicate its outputs. Typically, a student with a more lightweight architecture is chosen, enabling model compression without substantial loss in predictive quality. Under conventional setups, however, distillation is applied only at the level of final predictions, leaving the student unable to draw on the teacher's guidance for its internal components. This limitation motivated our investigation into distillation applied to intermediate layers. Because a strict one-to-one correspondence between student and teacher layers frequently does not exist, prior approaches address this by selecting only a subset of teacher layers and bypassing the rest—a compromise that directly degrades performance. In contrast, the proposed method introduces a combinatorial strategy grounded in attention mechanisms: teacher-side representations across layers are merged by weighting each layer according to its relative importance, and distillation is then carried out between these fused teacher representations and the corresponding student layers. To evaluate the proposed method, we compressed a 12-layer BERT (Devlin et al. 2019) into variants with 6, 4, and 2 layers and assessed their performance across GLUE tasks (Wang et al. 2018). The results demonstrate that the proposed combinatorial approach consistently surpasses existing distillation techniques.

author: Cameron
title: Compact Models Benefit Greatly from Pre-training: A Reassessment of Strong Baselines
abstract: Self-supervised pre-training on large general-domain corpora has driven recent advances in natural language representations, yet the resulting models are costly to deploy. This has motivated a line of concurrent work proposing model compression techniques for pre-trained language representations (Sun et al., 2019; Sanh, 2019). Notably absent from this literature, however, is a thorough evaluation of the straightforward baseline of simply pre-training and fine-tuning compact models directly. We demonstrate here that, even for smaller architectures, pre-training continues to matter substantially, and that fine-tuning compact pre-trained models can match more elaborate approaches from concurrent work. Building on this foundation, we investigate applying standard knowledge distillation to transfer task-specific knowledge from large fine-tuned models into these compact pre-trained models. This yields a simple, general, and effective procedure we call Pre-trained Distillation, which provides additional gains beyond pre-training alone. We then conduct extensive experiments examining how pre-training and distillation interact under two under-studied variables: the size of the model and the characteristics of unlabeled task data. A notable finding is that these two factors exhibit a compound effect even when applied sequentially on identical data. To support future work, we will publicly release our full set of 24 miniature pre-trained BERT models.

author: Parsons
title: Distillation of Dense Retrieval Models via a Curriculum-Based Training Strategy
abstract: Distilling ranking knowledge from a base re-ranking model into a dense retrieval model has been established by prior work as a reliable path to improved retrieval performance. We introduce a generic optimization framework grounded in curriculum learning principles, in which the difficulty of training data generated by the teacher model is systematically controlled throughout the distillation process. Rather than exposing the student model to all distillation data uniformly, the proposed method schedules increasingly demanding supervision: training begins with coarse-grained pairwise preferences among documents in the teacher's ranked list and advances progressively toward finer-grained document ordering requirements. This iterative procedure continuously updates the student model as the difficulty of the knowledge distillation signal escalates. To validate the approach, we apply a straightforward instantiation of the proposed method to two state-of-the-art dense retrieval models and evaluate across three publicly available passage retrieval benchmarks. The experimental results confirm the effectiveness of our framework.

author: Perez
title: Multi-Task Re-Learning Through Single-Task Distillation for Natural Language Understanding
abstract: Achieving multi-task neural networks that match or exceed the performance of their single-task counterparts remains a persistent challenge. We address this by employing knowledge distillation in which individually trained single-task models serve as teachers to guide a multi-task student model. To further strengthen this framework, we introduce teacher annealing, a novel technique that progressively shifts training from distillation toward supervised learning, enabling the multi-task student to surpass the single-task teachers. The proposed method is evaluated by fine-tuning BERT on the GLUE benchmark under a multi-task setting, and it yields consistent gains over both standard single-task and conventional multi-task training baselines.

author: Stewart
title: Knowledge Distillation as a Framework for Differentially Private Model Compression
abstract: Powerful deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly needed on mobile devices to satisfy the growing appetite for intelligent mobile applications. Yet the exceptional accuracy of DNNs depends on models of ever-growing complexity, whose computational demands far exceed what mobile devices can handle. Compounding this problem, building such sophisticated DNN models requires app service providers to collect and process large quantities of sensitive user data, and deploying these models directly on public mobile devices introduces unacceptable privacy risks. To enable on-device deep learning while addressing both capacity and privacy constraints, we propose a private model compression framework. Under the knowledge distillation paradigm, hint learning, distillation learning, and self learning are employed jointly to produce a compact, high-speed neural network. The knowledge transferred from the cumbersome teacher model is adaptively bounded and carefully perturbed to enforce differential privacy guarantees. We additionally introduce a query sample selection strategy that keeps query counts low and bounds privacy loss. Comprehensive experiments together with a deployment on an Android mobile device demonstrate that the proposed method efficiently compresses cumbersome models while delivering strong privacy protection. Specifically, on SVHN, under a meaningful $(9.83, 10^{-6})$-differential privacy guarantee, the student model yielded by the proposed method achieves a 20$\times$ compression ratio and 19$\times$ speed-up, with only 0.97% degradation in accuracy.

author: Adams
title: Does Label Smoothing Actually Conflict with Knowledge Distillation? An Empirical Investigation
abstract: The goal of this paper is to empirically examine a recently proposed claim that label smoothing and knowledge distillation are fundamentally at odds. We first explain the reasoning by which this conflict was originally identified — specifically, that label smoothing destroys relative information encoded among teacher logits. A novel analysis is then presented showing how label smoothing shapes the distributions of classes that are semantically close versus semantically distant. We further introduce a quantitative metric designed to measure how much information has been erased from a sample's representation. Building on this, we conduct extensive analyses, visualizations, and experiments across Image Classification, Binary Networks, and Neural Machine Translation to demonstrate the limitations and one-sidedness of the incompatibility viewpoint. We conclude with a broad discussion of specific conditions under which label smoothing does genuinely diminish its own effectiveness. Project page: http://zhiqiangshen.com/projects/LS_and_KD/index.html.

author: Clark
title: Knowledge Distillation as a Foundation for Architecture-Independent Federated Learning
abstract: Can a universal API be constructed for federated learning in which an ad-hoc collection of data-holders (agents) engage in collaborative training without any assumptions about the model architecture each agent employs and without access to representative public data? Knowledge distillation (KD) naturally emerges as the primary mechanism for building such protocols. Yet, counterintuitively, we demonstrate that the most straightforward KD-based federated learning protocols yield poor performance. To understand this failure, we introduce a new theoretical framework — Federated Kernel ridge regression — capable of jointly capturing both data heterogeneity and model heterogeneity. Our theoretical analysis reveals that performance degradation stems primarily from a fundamental limitation inherent to knowledge distillation when data heterogeneity is present. Building on this framework, we analyze existing approaches and derive new KD-based protocols. Experiments on real-world tasks with neural networks confirm that, while performance remains unsatisfactory, the empirical results closely align with what our theoretical framework predicts.

author: Hahn
title: A General Object Detection Distillation Framework Using Pearson Correlation Coefficient
abstract: Although knowledge distillation (KD) is a broadly adopted approach for producing lightweight object detectors, how to effectively distill across heterogeneous detector architectures remains insufficiently explored. Through empirical investigation, we demonstrate that FPN features of higher quality from a heterogeneous teacher detector benefit the student even when their detection heads and label assignment strategies differ. Nevertheless, naively minimizing the discrepancy between teacher and student feature maps introduces two distinct difficulties. First, disparities in feature magnitude between teacher and student impose excessively rigid constraints on the student's learning. Second, FPN stages and channels in which the teacher exhibits large feature magnitudes tend to dominate the distillation loss gradient, overwhelming the contribution of other features and injecting substantial noise into the KD process. The proposed method addresses both issues by matching features via Pearson Correlation Coefficient, which directs attention toward relational information in the teacher's representations while relaxing any strict requirements on feature magnitude. Evaluated across both homogeneous and heterogeneous student-teacher pairs, the proposed method consistently surpasses existing detection KD approaches and additionally offers faster convergence. Using a MaskRCNN-Swin detector as a powerful teacher, a ResNet-50-based RetinaNet reaches 41.5% mAP and a ResNet-50-based FCOS reaches 43.9% mAP on COCO2017, representing gains of 4.1% and 4.8% over their respective baselines.

author: Walter
title: Distilling Effectively from High-Performing Teacher Models
abstract: While prior knowledge distillation approaches have concentrated on baseline settings in which teacher models and training strategies are comparatively weak and fall short of state-of-the-art performance, the proposed method is specifically designed to enable effective distillation from a stronger teacher. Through empirical investigation, we observe that when the teacher is considerably stronger, the gap between its predictions and those of the student tends to become substantially larger. Consequently, enforcing an exact alignment of predictions via KL divergence disrupts the training process and causes existing distillation methods to degrade significantly. We demonstrate that retaining the relational structure among teacher and student predictions is sufficient, and introduce a correlation-based loss that explicitly captures the intrinsic inter-class relations present in the teacher's output. Furthermore, since individual instances bear varying degrees of semantic similarity to each class, we extend this relational matching principle to the intra-class level as well. The proposed method is straightforward yet effective; thorough experiments show that it generalizes consistently across diverse architectures, model sizes, and training strategies, reaching state-of-the-art performance on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation benchmarks. Code is available at: https://github.com/hunto/DIST_KD .

author: Edwards
title: Cross-Domain Knowledge Distillation for Communication-Efficient and Privacy-Preserving Federated Learning
abstract: In Federated Learning (FL), a global model is trained collaboratively across local nodes while keeping all training data decentralized. To handle unbalanced data distribution, existing FL approaches commonly share model parameters or rely on co-distillation, yet these strategies are hindered by communication bottlenecks and, more critically, expose the system to privacy leakage risks. We introduce a communication-efficient, privacy-preserving approach within a FL framework that leverages one-shot offline knowledge distillation over unlabeled public data drawn from a different domain. To achieve stronger privacy guarantees without degrading accuracy, the proposed method aggregates local predictions from fully trained local models into a quantized, noisy ensemble. Through extensive experiments spanning image classification and text classification benchmarks, we demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses baseline FL algorithms, achieving superior results in both predictive accuracy and communication efficiency.

author: Rios
title: Knowledge Distillation as a Tool for Enhancing Neural Topic Models
abstract: Large document collections are frequently analyzed using topic models, which surface human-interpretable topics that aid comprehension. By leveraging knowledge distillation, we integrate the complementary strengths of probabilistic topic models and pretrained transformers. The proposed method is modular and can be readily incorporated into any neural topic model to enhance topic quality; we validate this across two models with substantially different architectures, achieving state-of-the-art topic coherence. Beyond improvements in aggregate performance across all estimated topics—the metric most commonly reported—we demonstrate that the proposed method also yields gains in direct head-to-head comparisons of aligned topics.

author: Foster
title: CTR Prediction via Knowledge Distillation from Teacher Ensembles
abstract: Deep learning approaches to click-through rate (CTR) prediction have attracted substantial research attention and delivered accuracy gains across numerous industrial systems. Yet the dominant research direction has been the design of increasingly elaborate network architectures aimed at capturing complex feature interactions and evolving user behaviors, with the consequence that growing model complexity imposes latency costs that impede deployment in real-time settings. Our work takes a different direction, proposing a model training strategy grounded in knowledge distillation (KD)—a teacher-student framework in which knowledge acquired by a teacher model is transferred to a student model. This KD-based strategy enables the student to be a simple vanilla DNN while still surpassing state-of-the-art teacher models in prediction accuracy. Motivated by these advantages, we extend the framework to leverage a powerful ensemble of teachers to further improve student model training. Several novel techniques tailored to ensembled CTR prediction are also introduced, among them teacher gating and an early stopping criterion driven by distillation loss. We carry out thorough experiments comparing the proposed method against 12 baseline models on three industrial datasets. Results from both offline evaluation and online A/B testing confirm the effectiveness of the proposed KD-based training strategy.

author: Rocha
title: Network Compression Under Few-Shot Constraints via a Cross Distillation Strategy
abstract: Deep neural networks can be made lightweight through model compression, yet the majority of well-established techniques depend on fine-tuning over large training sets to maintain accuracy — a requirement that conflicts with privacy and security constraints. This paper examines a middle ground between these competing concerns: few shot network compression, which asks how a network can be compressed effectively, with minimal accuracy degradation, when only a small number of samples per class are available. The fundamental difficulty is that, with so few training instances, the compressed network tends to over-fit, producing high estimation errors relative to the original network's behavior at inference time. These errors accumulate as they propagate through successive layers, ultimately degrading the final network output. We address this by introducing cross distillation, a layer-wise knowledge distillation technique in which the hidden layers of the teacher and student networks are interleaved, thereby suppressing the layer-wise accumulation of estimation errors. The proposed method constitutes a general framework that is compatible with widely used compression approaches such as pruning. Thorough evaluation on standard benchmark datasets shows that cross distillation yields substantial gains in student network accuracy under few-shot conditions.

author: Ellis
title: Global Topology Alignment for Knowledge Distillation in Graph Neural Networks
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) that are lightweight and resource-efficient can be trained more effectively by leveraging knowledge distillation from larger, more expressive teacher models. Prior distillation work for GNNs introduced the Local Structure Preserving loss (LSP), which enforces consistency between teacher and student node embeddings by matching local structural relationships along edges. Because real-world graphs frequently exhibit noisy edges and latent interactions, this paper investigates whether aligning the global topology of teacher-learned graph representations yields a more effective distillation objective than local structure matching. To this end, the proposed method—Graph Contrastive Representation Distillation (G-CRD)—employs contrastive learning to implicitly enforce global topology preservation by pulling student node embeddings toward teacher node embeddings within a shared representation space. We further contribute an expanded benchmark suite drawn from large-scale real-world datasets, specifically targeting settings where a meaningful performance gap between teacher and student GNNs exists. Evaluated across 4 datasets and 14 heterogeneous GNN architectures, G-CRD consistently improves both the performance and robustness of lightweight GNNs, surpassing LSP, a global structure preserving variant of LSP, and distillation baselines originating from 2D computer vision. Analysis of representational similarity between teacher and student embedding spaces demonstrates that G-CRD achieves a balance between preserving local and global relationships, whereas structure preserving methods tend to excel at one at the expense of the other. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/chaitjo/efficient-gnns

author: Baker
title: Breathing New Life into Rare Words: Fully Exploiting Bilingual Corpora for Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: Training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models commonly relies on synthetic data produced via knowledge distillation (KD). Nevertheless, a gap exists between distilled and original corpora with respect to low-frequency words, which causes the model to make more prediction errors on such words. To address this issue, we incorporate raw parallel data directly into NAT training by means of pretraining. Through an examination of directed alignments, we observe that KD causes low-frequency source words to align with target words more deterministically, yet it fails to produce adequate alignments from target to source for low-frequency items. To remedy this, we introduce reverse KD as a way to recover alignments for low-frequency target words. We then unify authentic and synthetic data by treating these two complementary techniques as a joint training strategy, thereby further improving NAT performance. Experiments are carried out across five translation benchmarks using two competitive architectures. The results show that the proposed method consistently and substantially reduces translation errors on low-frequency words, yielding broad improvements in translation quality. Notably, scores of 28.2 and 33.9 BLEU points are attained on WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English, respectively. Code, data, and trained models are publicly released at \url{https://github.com/alphadl/RLFW-NAT}.

author: Wright
title: Comprehensive Video Scene Parsing via Semantics Learned Through Distillation
abstract: Autonomous systems fundamentally require complete perception of their environment. It has been demonstrated by recent research that geometry (depth) and motion (optical flow) can be acquired by deep neural networks from monocular video without ground truth annotations, which are especially difficult to obtain for these two tasks. Jointly learning depth and motion together with semantics using a monocular camera represents the additional stride toward holistic scene understanding taken in this work, where supervision for semantics is delivered by proxy ground truth images generated through a pre-trained network acting as a distillation source. The three tasks are addressed simultaneously through: a) a training protocol combining knowledge distillation with self-supervision, and b) a compact network architecture that supports efficient scene understanding on both power-hungry GPUs and resource-constrained embedded platforms. Extensive evaluation of the proposed method demonstrates that it achieves state-of-the-art results across monocular depth estimation, optical flow, and motion segmentation.

author: Hoffman
title: Distillation-Based Approaches to Federated Learning
abstract: Rather than exposing raw data, distributed learning frameworks typically operate by transmitting model parameters among participating workers—federated learning being the canonical instance, wherein gradients or weights of each neural network are shared. For modern deep neural networks with vast numbers of model parameters, however, the communication overhead of this approach becomes prohibitive under constrained bandwidth. Federated distillation (FD) addresses this by exchanging only model outputs, whose dimensionality is generally far smaller than the number of model parameters (e.g., 10 labels in the MNIST dataset), making it a highly promising distributed learning alternative. This chapter aims to develop a thorough understanding of FD and to establish both its communication efficiency and its applicability across diverse tasks. Toward that end, the first part analytically demystifies FD's operating principles by presenting a novel asymptotic treatment of two fundamental algorithms—knowledge distillation (KD) and co-distillation (CD)—through the lens of neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory. The second part then details a reference implementation of FD on a classification problem, benchmarking its accuracy and communication efficiency against FL. Finally, the third part extends the scope to two representative application scenarios that highlight FD's versatility: FD operating over asymmetric uplink-and-downlink wireless channels, and FD applied to reinforcement learning.

author: Baker
title: Merging Heterogeneous Classifiers into a Unified Model via Distillation
abstract: We address the task of consolidating knowledge from multiple classifiers—each trained on distinct architectures and disjoint sets of target classes—into one unified classifier, using only a generic collection of unlabelled data. Referred to here as the heterogeneous classifier unification problem, this setting arises naturally when data originates from several independent sources that, for reasons such as privacy constraints, are unable to exchange raw data and can only share their privately trained models. Furthermore, individual sources may lack sufficient data to cover all classes, and differences in available computational resources may prevent them from adopting a common classification model. Our solution extends knowledge distillation to the setting of merging such heterogeneous classifiers. We establish a probabilistic relationship linking the outputs of these heterogeneous classifiers to a joint probability distribution spanning all classes. Building on this relationship, the proposed method introduces two families of approaches—one grounded in cross-entropy minimisation and the other in matrix factorisation—that together enable the estimation of soft labels across all classes from unlabelled samples; these soft labels are then used in place of ground truth supervision to train the unified classifier. Through extensive experimentation on the ImageNet, LSUN, and Places365 datasets, we demonstrate that the proposed method substantially outperforms a straightforward distillation baseline and attains accuracy approaching that of classifiers trained with full supervision in a centralised setting.

author: Richards
title: Knowledge Distillation and Generative Adversarial Networks for Text Generation
abstract: Many NLP tasks—including machine translation, text summarization, and language modeling—depend critically on high-quality text generation. While GANs have produced impressive results in computer vision image synthesis, applying them with comparable success to NLP is substantially harder because of the discrete nature of textual data. We present a method that leverages knowledge distillation to effectively harness a GAN framework for generating text. Autoencoders (AEs) are employed to produce continuous sentence representations—smooth distributions that assign non-zero probability mass to multiple words simultaneously—and distillation of these representations is used to guide generator training toward synthesizing comparably smooth outputs. Across multiple datasets, experiments validate our approach, demonstrating superior performance in BLEU score and Jensen-Shannon distance (JSD) relative to conventional GAN-based text generation baselines that do not use pre-training.

author: Hurst
title: Learning Efficient Ranking Models for Recommender Systems via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: We introduce an approach to knowledge distillation (KD) tailored specifically for learning to rank settings, referred to here as the proposed method. A compact student model is trained to rank items/documents by drawing supervision from both the labeled training data and the outputs of a larger teacher model, enabling the student model to attain ranking performance comparable to the teacher while requiring substantially less computation at inference time due to its reduced model size. Unlike prior KD work demonstrated in image recognition, the proposed method addresses the particular challenges that arise in ranking problems. A key advantage is flexibility: the proposed method is orthogonal to the specific choice of ranking models used for either the teacher or the student. Evaluations conducted on public datasets using state-of-the-art recommendation models confirm that the proposed method fulfills its design objectives—a student model trained with the proposed method achieves ranking performance close to that of the teacher model and substantially better than a student model trained without it, all while maintaining a model size that is less than half that of the teacher model.

author: Ross
title: Distilling Ensembles and Oracle Systems for Improved Neural Machine Translation
abstract: A student network can be trained to achieve higher performance by learning from a stronger teacher network, a technique known as knowledge distillation. Because decoding with a Neural Machine Translation (NMT) engine is computationally costly, reducing model size can substantially accelerate inference. We show that the translation quality of both an ensemble teacher and an oracle BLEU teacher can be successfully transferred into a single NMT model. We also demonstrate translation gains obtained from a teacher network that shares the same architecture and dimensions as the student network. Since training the student model remains computationally demanding, we propose a data filtering approach driven by teacher model knowledge, which both reduces training time and yields improvements in translation quality. The proposed method requires no modifications to existing code and can be straightforwardly applied to any NMT architecture to accelerate the decoding process.

author: Robinson
title: Diagnosing and Correcting Low-Frequency Word Selection in Non-Autoregressive Translation
abstract: Training non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models relies critically on knowledge distillation (KD), which simplifies raw data through an autoregressive teacher model. Through empirical investigation, we demonstrate that this training procedure carries an unintended consequence: lexical choice errors associated with low-frequency words are transferred from the teacher model into the NAT model. To address this issue, the proposed method incorporates raw data directly into NAT training, recovering information about low-frequency words that is absent from the distilled data. Concretely, an additional Kullback-Leibler divergence term is introduced, computed by contrasting the lexical choice distribution of the NAT model against that encoded in the raw data. Evaluations spanning multiple language pairs and model architectures establish both the effectiveness and broad applicability of the proposed method. Thorough analyses validate our hypothesis that performance gains stem from a reduction in lexical choice errors on low-frequency words. Notably, the proposed method advances state-of-the-art NAT results on the WMT14 English-German and WMT16 Romanian-English datasets to 27.8 and 33.8 BLEU points, respectively. Code will be made publicly available.

author: Bright
title: Bridging the Gap to Real-World Lipreading via Knowledge Distillation and Lightweight Architectures
abstract: Neural network-driven lipreading has advanced considerably in recent years, with prior efforts largely directed at architecture search and generalization improvements. Yet a substantial divide remains between existing approaches and what is actually needed for lipreading to function effectively in real-world deployment settings. We introduce a set of contributions that collectively close much of this divide. First, self-distillation is employed to push state-of-the-art accuracy to 88.5% on LRW and 46.6% on LRW-1000, representing a substantial improvement over prior best results. Second, several architectural modifications are proposed, among them a novel Depthwise Separable Temporal Convolutional Network (DS-TCN) head, which together reduce the computational burden to a small fraction of that required by the already relatively efficient baseline. Third, knowledge distillation is demonstrated to be a highly effective mechanism for recovering the accuracy lost when transitioning to these lightweight architectures. The outcome is a family of models spanning a range of accuracy–efficiency operating points. Notably, the most compelling lightweight models match current state-of-the-art performance while achieving reductions of 8.2x and 3.9x in computational cost and parameter count, respectively—advances that we anticipate will make practical deployment of lipreading systems a realistic prospect.

author: Hicks
title: Adapting Through Teaching: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Domain Adaptation
abstract: Many real-world settings require models to generalize across data distributions that shift between training and inference, making domain adaptation a critical challenge. Existing deep learning methods address this by training simultaneously on source and target domain data, which becomes impractical when adaptation must occur across many domains or when a domain changes over time—as in spam detection, where adversaries perpetually evolve their strategies. We address this limitation by introducing an extension of Knowledge Distillation (Bucilua et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015) to the domain adaptation setting, which we term Knowledge Adaptation. By leveraging the domain-specific knowledge encoded in multiple teachers alongside inter-domain similarity, a student model trained under this framework attains state-of-the-art results on unsupervised multi-source domain adaptation on a standard sentiment analysis benchmark. In the single-teacher setting, however, domain similarity alone proves insufficient as a proxy for the teacher's reliability on the target domain. We therefore introduce a straightforward metric that exhibits strong correlation with teacher accuracy in the target domain, and show that using it to select high-confidence examples for student training yields state-of-the-art performance in the single-source adaptation scenario.

author: Williams
title: Data-Free Student-Teacher Alignment Through Adversarial Generator Optimization
abstract: Knowledge distillation—compressing a large teacher network into a smaller student—is widely used throughout contemporary deep learning. Yet as training datasets grow larger and data privacy requirements become more stringent, access to the original training data for the teacher is frequently unavailable. We introduce the proposed method, which enables a student to match its teacher's predictions without requiring any data or metadata whatsoever. A generator is trained adversarially to discover images on which the student's predictions diverge most from the teacher's; these images are then used to update the student. On straightforward benchmarks such as SVHN, the resulting student closely replicates teacher behavior, and on CIFAR10 the proposed method surpasses the current state-of-the-art for few-shot distillation (100 images per class) despite operating with zero training data. We further introduce a metric that measures the degree of belief matching between teacher and student in the neighborhood of decision boundaries. This metric reveals that our zero-shot student achieves a substantially higher match with the teacher than a student distilled using real data does. Code is available at: https://github.com/polo5/ZeroShotKnowledgeTransfer

author: Rodriguez
title: Beyond Graph Neural Network Boundaries: A Knowledge Distillation Framework for Effective Graph Learning
abstract: Graph-based semi-supervised learning represents a significant challenge in the machine learning community. Although GNN-based classification approaches have demonstrated clear advantages over classical techniques like label propagation in recent years, the intricate architectures underlying these models give rise to complex prediction mechanisms that fail to fully exploit valuable prior knowledge inherent in the data — for instance, the tendency of structurally correlated nodes to share the same class label. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a knowledge distillation-based framework in which the knowledge encoded in any pre-trained GNN teacher model is extracted and transferred into a purpose-built student model. This student model combines two straightforward prediction mechanisms — feature transformation and label propagation — which inherently preserve feature-based and structure-based prior knowledge, respectively. Concretely, the student model is formulated as a trainable, parameterized combination of these two modules. Consequently, the resulting student is able to leverage both the prior knowledge embedded in its design and the knowledge acquired from GNN teachers, yielding more accurate predictions. An additional benefit is that the student model exhibits a considerably more interpretable prediction process relative to GNNs. Across five public benchmark datasets and using seven teacher models — GCN, GAT, APPNP, SAGE, SGC, GCNII, and GLP — our experiments demonstrate that the student model consistently surpasses its corresponding teacher by an average margin of 1.4%–4.7%. Code and data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/CPF

author: Burton
title: Hardware-Aware Block-Structured Pruning for Compact Transformer-Based Language Models at Scale
abstract: High accuracy across numerous natural language processing (NLP) tasks has been increasingly achieved by large-scale pre-trained language models. Nevertheless, their adoption—particularly in edge computing scenarios—is hindered by the memory footprint and inference speed constraints of real hardware platforms. We present a transformer-based large-scale language representation approach that attains efficiency through block-structured pruning designed with hardware compatibility in mind. To drive the optimization, reweighted group Lasso is integrated into the block-structured pruning framework. Beyond the substantial reductions in both weight storage and computation, high compression rates are attained by the proposed method. Evaluated across BERT, RoBERTa, and DistilBERT on General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark tasks, the proposed method delivers compression of up to 5.0x with zero or negligible accuracy degradation on select task(s). Furthermore, the proposed method is orthogonal to existing compact pre-trained models such as DistilBERT obtained via knowledge distillation: an additional average compression rate of 1.79x can be realized on top of DistilBERT while incurring zero or minor accuracy loss. The resulting compressed models are well suited for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.

author: Conner
title: Transferring BERT's Task-Specific Representations to Lightweight Neural Networks via Distillation
abstract: A prevailing trend in natural language processing research has been the rapid growth in model depth and architectural complexity. Deep language representation models such as BERT, ELMo, and GPT exemplify this trajectory, and their success has fostered a widespread belief that simpler, shallower neural network architectures are no longer viable for language understanding tasks. We challenge this assumption by showing that basic, computationally inexpensive neural networks can be brought to a competitive level of performance without modifying their architecture, incorporating external training data, or introducing additional input features. The proposed method transfers knowledge distilled from BERT—a leading language representation model—into a single-layer BiLSTM for sentence-level tasks and into its siamese variant for sentence-pair tasks. Evaluated across paraphrasing, natural language inference, and sentiment classification benchmarks, the proposed method attains results comparable to ELMo while requiring approximately 100 times fewer parameters and reducing inference time by a factor of roughly 15.

author: Henderson
title: Accelerating Node Classification at Inference Time: Distilling Graph Neural Networks into Graph-Free MLPs
abstract: Multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) require no graph dependency at inference time and therefore run substantially faster than Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), yet they typically underperform GNNs on node classification tasks. GNNs, by contrast, achieve strong node classification results across many benchmarks but face significant scalability challenges in industrial deployments, because inference must access neighbor nodes across multiple hops, introducing unacceptable latency in time-sensitive applications. Techniques such as pruning and quantization reduce Multiplication-and-ACcumulation (MAC) operations and can accelerate GNNs, but the fundamental data dependency remains unresolved, limiting the gains they provide. Given these complementary trade-offs, the proposed method bridges GNNs and MLPs through knowledge distillation (KD), transferring the predictive capacity of a GNN teacher into an MLP student that carries no graph dependency at inference time. Experiments conducted under a production setting that covers both transductive and inductive prediction scenarios across 7 datasets demonstrate that the distilled MLPs improve over stand-alone MLPs by 12.36% on average and match GNN accuracy on 6/7 datasets. Relative to GNNs, the proposed distilled MLPs achieve inference speedups of 146X–273X, and relative to other acceleration methods the speedups reach 14X–27X, while retaining competitive accuracy. A thorough analysis identifies the conditions under which distilled MLPs can closely match GNN performance, supporting their adoption as a practical, low-latency alternative in deployment-constrained environments.

author: Brown
title: A Joint Framework for Compressing Vision Transformers via Pruning, Layer Skipping, and Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Recently, vision transformers (ViTs) have attracted growing interest. Despite relying on no image-specific operators like convolutions, ViTs achieve competitive accuracy when trained at scale on large datasets. Nevertheless, the cost of inference remains high, largely because of repeatedly stacked multi-head self-attention modules and related components. While compressing convolutional neural networks has been extensively studied with considerable success, compression of vision transformers is a newer research direction, and prior efforts have addressed only one or two compression dimensions at a time. The proposed method introduces a unified compression framework for ViTs that tightly integrates three complementary techniques: pruning, layer skipping, and knowledge distillation. Under a distillation loss, the approach jointly optimizes model weights, per-layer pruning ratios and masks, and layer-skip configurations within a budget-constrained, end-to-end formulation. The resulting optimization problem is solved with the primal-dual algorithm. Evaluated across multiple ViT architectures—including DeiT and T2T-ViT backbones on ImageNet—the proposed method consistently surpasses recent competing approaches. As one concrete illustration, DeiT-Tiny can be reduced to 50% of its original FLOPs with negligible accuracy degradation. Code is publicly available at: \url{https://github.com/VITA-Group/UVC}.

author: James
title: Cross-Modal Contrastive Learning with Iterative Self-Distillation for Robust Representations
abstract: Web-crawled image captioning datasets exhibit noisy many-to-many correspondences that CLIP's training objective fails to adequately handle, resulting in poor data and compute efficiency. We propose a training framework grounded in cross-modal contrastive learning that addresses this limitation by combining progressive self-distillation with soft image-text alignments, enabling more efficient learning of robust representations from such noisy data. In each minibatch, the model leverages its own distilled knowledge to dynamically produce soft-alignment targets for a subset of image-caption pairs, which are subsequently used to drive parameter updates. Evaluation spanning 14 benchmark datasets demonstrates that the proposed method consistently surpasses its CLIP counterpart across multiple settings—namely (a) zero-shot classification, (b) linear probe transfer, and (c) image-text retrieval—while introducing no additional computational overhead. Robustness analysis conducted via an ImageNet-based test-bed indicates that the proposed method achieves superior effective robustness against natural distribution shifts relative to both ImageNet-trained models and CLIP. Furthermore, pretraining experiments conducted on datasets varying across two orders of magnitude in scale reveal that performance gains over CLIP tend to grow with the number of training examples.

author: Ferrell
title: Supernet Training via Alpha-Divergence Minimization for Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Weight-sharing neural architecture search (NAS) is a powerful approach for automating the design of efficient neural networks. A supernet is constructed to encompass all candidate architectures as sub-networks, and both the supernet and its sub-networks are optimized jointly. A critical factor in the effectiveness of weight-sharing NAS is how well knowledge is distilled from the supernet into the sub-networks. We identify a shortcoming of KL divergence—the standard distillation divergence in common use—namely that it causes student sub-networks to either over-estimate or under-estimate the uncertainty of the teacher supernet, degrading sub-network performance. To address this, we introduce a training strategy for supernets grounded in the more general alpha-divergence framework. Through adaptive selection of the alpha parameter, the proposed method simultaneously avoids over-estimation and under-estimation of the teacher model's uncertainty. We apply this alpha-divergence based supernet training to slimmable neural networks as well as to weight-sharing NAS, achieving substantial gains in both settings. The resulting model family outperforms prior-art architectures—including BigNAS, Once-for-All networks, and AttentiveNAS—across a broad range of FLOPs regimes, attaining 80.0% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet at just 444M FLOPs. Code and pretrained models are publicly released at https://github.com/facebookresearch/AlphaNet.

author: Rice
title: Fake Media Detection Across Domains via Continual Learning and Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Despite remarkable progress in artificial intelligence over recent decades, most AI models remain dependent on static datasets collected under fixed conditions. Sequential learning from a non-stationary, continuous stream of related data — analogous to how biological organisms acquire knowledge — is the focus of the growing continual learning research area. A parallel concern in modern multimedia is the proliferation of fabricated content, including deepfakes and GAN-generated synthetic face imagery. While many recently introduced detection approaches achieve strong accuracy, their dependence on fixed datasets and constrained evaluation protocols remains a serious limitation. To address this, the proposed method integrates continual learning into the training dynamics of neural networks, with particular emphasis on substantially improving data efficiency. Specifically, the proposed method unifies continual learning, representation learning, and knowledge distillation within a single framework, designed to carry out sequential domain adaptation across new deepfake and GAN-generated synthetic face datasets. Catastrophic forgetting is effectively mitigated through a teacher-student model architecture. Comprehensive experimental evaluation shows that the proposed method successfully adapts across domains to detect low-quality deepfake videos and GAN-generated images from multiple datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art baseline methods.

author: Maddox
title: Many-to-Many Layer Mapping for BERT Compression via Earth Mover's Distance
abstract: Although pre-trained language models such as BERT have delivered remarkable performance across a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, their substantial memory footprints and computational demands make deployment on resource-constrained devices highly challenging. We introduce a distillation approach for BERT in which every intermediate student layer is permitted to draw knowledge from any combination of intermediate teacher layers, enabling many-to-many layer mapping. This flexibility allows the student network to adaptively learn from different teacher layers depending on the requirements of each NLP task. To quantify the minimum total cost of transferring knowledge from the teacher network to the student network under this mapping scheme, we employ Earth Mover's Distance (EMD), which provides an effective means of aligning layers in the many-to-many setting. Beyond this, we present a cost attention mechanism that automatically determines the layer weights used within EMD, with the dual benefit of boosting model performance and reducing convergence time. Comprehensive evaluations on the GLUE benchmark show that the proposed method achieves competitive results relative to strong baseline methods in both accuracy and degree of model compression.

author: Valencia
title: A Survey on Model Compression Techniques for Deep Learning in Text Applications
abstract: Deep learning architectures—including Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTMs) networks, and Transformer [120]-based models such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [24], Generative Pre-training Transformer (GPT-2) [94], Multi-task Deep Neural Network (MT-DNN) [73], Extra-Long Network (XLNet) [134], Text-to-text transfer transformer (T5) [95], T-NLG [98], and GShard [63]—have driven remarkable advances across natural language processing (NLP) and information retrieval (IR). Nevertheless, these models carry enormous parameter counts, whereas practical deployment scenarios impose strict constraints on model size, inference latency, and energy consumption. This survey examines six categories of compression approaches—Pruning, Quantization, Knowledge Distillation, Parameter Sharing, Tensor Decomposition, and Sub-quadratic Transformer based methods—through which such large models can be made suitable for real-world industrial NLP systems. The volume of recently published research in this space, combined with the pressing practical need for efficient, compact models, motivates the present work, which we believe synthesizes the substantial contributions of the deep learning for NLP community over the past several years into a unified and coherent narrative.

author: Smith
title: Compressing Generative Adversarial Networks via Neural Architecture Search and Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Growing demand for running Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) on mobile devices—for tasks including image translation, enhancement, and editing—has brought GAN compression into the spotlight. Yet relative to the substantial body of work on compressing other deep models, research on compressing GANs (typically their generators) remains at an early stage. Current GAN compression methods are restricted to particular GAN architectures and loss formulations. Drawing on recent advances in AutoML for deep model compression, we incorporate AutoML into the GAN compression pipeline and propose an automated search-and-distillation framework. The proposed method operates over a carefully constructed efficient search space, conducting end-to-end architecture discovery for new lightweight generators under specified computational resource budgets. Knowledge distillation from the original GAN model guides the search process, simultaneously achieving compression. The proposed method is entirely automatic, standalone—requiring no trained discriminators—and broadly applicable across diverse GAN models. We assess the framework on two representative GAN benchmarks: image translation and super resolution. Without additional tricks, the proposed method produces remarkably compact models that are also more competitive, substantially outperforming existing compression alternatives. Code and pretrained models are publicly available at https://github.com/TAMU-VITA/AGD.

author: Le
title: Rethinking How Video and Pose Representations Interact for Daily Activity Recognition
abstract: Recognizing Activities of Daily Living (ADL) is challenging because such actions frequently appear visually similar, demanding that models capture fine-grained details for reliable discrimination. Although methods that fuse RGB with 3D poses dominate this area—partly because recent 3D ConvNets are too inflexible to pick up subtle motion patterns within an action—obtaining 3D poses from an RGB stream incurs substantial computational cost whenever dedicated sensors are unavailable, constraining the applicability of such pipelines in latency-sensitive real-world settings. Given this constraint, the central question becomes: what is the optimal strategy for exploiting 3D poses in ADL recognition? We address this by proposing two distinct extensions to a pose-driven attention mechanism known as the Video-Pose Network (VPN). The first direction transfers pose knowledge into RGB representations via feature-level distillation, while the second replicates pose-driven attention patterns through attention-level distillation. Both directions are then unified within a single framework, yielding the proposed method. Experiments on 4 public datasets demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses representative baselines regardless of whether 3D poses are available at inference time, while also delivering substantial speed gains and robust tolerance to noisy poses. Code is publicly released at https://github.com/srijandas07/vpnplusplus.

author: Maldonado
title: Feature-Level Imitation as a Superior Paradigm for Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) enables compact student networks to be trained more effectively by leveraging the guidance of high-capacity teacher networks. Conventional approaches supervise the student using the teacher's soft logits as an auxiliary training signal. We contend, instead, that directing the student to mimic the teacher's features at the penultimate layer yields greater benefits. Beyond allowing the student to absorb richer information directly from the teacher features, this feature mimicking strategy remains applicable even when the teacher has been trained without a softmax layer—a setting where soft logits are unavailable. Empirical results demonstrate that this approach surpasses traditional KD in terms of accuracy. To refine the feature mimicking process further, we decompose each feature vector into two components: its magnitude and its direction. We argue that the student feature's magnitude should be given greater latitude by the teacher, while the student's primary focus should be on replicating the feature direction. Motivated by this, the proposed method introduces a loss term grounded in locality-sensitive hashing (LSH). This loss term causes the proposed method to mimic feature directions more faithfully, while relaxing constraints imposed on feature magnitudes, ultimately reaching state-of-the-art distillation accuracy. We offer theoretical analyses explaining how LSH promotes accurate feature direction mimicking, and we additionally demonstrate the generality of feature mimicking by extending it to multi-label recognition and object detection tasks.

author: Herrera
title: Knowledge Distillation as a Framework for GAN Compression
abstract: Domain transfer, super resolution, and synthetic data generation are among the machine learning applications in which Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have seen widespread adoption. Deployment of leading GANs is costly on low SWAP (size, weight, and power) platforms such as mobile devices, as well as in real-time settings, owing to parameter counts that frequently reach tens of millions. No prior work has addressed reducing the parameter count of GANs. We therefore introduce a compression approach grounded in knowledge distillation, whereby a compact student GAN is trained to replicate the behavior of a larger teacher GAN. Using the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Celeb-A datasets, the proposed method achieves teacher-to-student compression ratios of 1669:1, 58:1, and 87:1, respectively, with no meaningful degradation in generated image quality. Our experiments reveal a qualitative boundary beyond which GAN compression is no longer viable. Additionally, when operating under an identical parameter budget, GANs compressed via the proposed method surpass GANs trained from scratch using conventional training procedures. We attribute this advantage in part to the optimization landscape of over-parameterized GANs, which is amenable to efficient training through alternating gradient descent. Consequently, first training an over-parameterized GAN and then applying the proposed compression scheme yields a generative model that is both high quality and highly compact.

author: Davidson
title: Knowledge Distillation from Multiple Viewpoints for Resilient Re-Identification
abstract: In Video-To-Video Re-Identification, robustness is commonly achieved by exploiting tracking data, yet this approach suffers a severe performance collapse when queries consist of single images (i.e., the Image-To-Video setting). Prior works have attempted to mitigate this degradation by distilling temporal knowledge from a Video-based network into an Image-based one. We instead propose a training strategy in which the knowledge transferred to the student originates from a collection of views that depict the same target object, a richer source of supervision than temporal information alone. Within a teacher-student framework, the proposed method uses this visual diversity as a supervisory signal, with the teacher guiding a student that has access to a reduced number of views at inference time. The student trained in this way surpasses both its teacher and the current state-of-the-art on Image-To-Video Re-Identification by a substantial margin — specifically 6.3% mAP on MARS, 8.6% on Duke-Video-ReId, and 5% on VeRi-776. Extensive experiments spanning Person, Vehicle, and Animal Re-ID evaluate the proposed method from both qualitative and quantitative perspectives, providing a thorough characterization of its properties. Code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/aimagelab/VKD.

author: Rodriguez
title: Graph Neural Network Publication under Differential Privacy Constraints
abstract: Privacy risks associated with trained graph neural networks (GNNs) have attracted growing attention as GNNs are increasingly deployed in sensitive domains such as medicine and healthcare. In particular, trained GNNs remain susceptible to attacks including membership inference even when adversaries are restricted to black-box model access. We introduce a centralized, privacy-preserving framework for publicly releasing GNN models, built on the assumption that an unlabeled public graph is available. The proposed method enables GNN models to be trained on public data while incorporating knowledge derived from private data, all within a privacy-preserving regime. To guarantee rigorous privacy, the proposed method integrates the knowledge distillation framework with two noise mechanisms—random subsampling and noisy labeling. A theoretical analysis of the approach is conducted within the Rényi differential privacy framework. Furthermore, strong empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms several baselines adapted to graph-structured data. Code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/iyempissy/privGnn.

author: Graham
title: Federated Learning Stabilization Through Hierarchical Multi-Branch Architectural Regularization
abstract: Data heterogeneity and imbalance among clients represent a fundamental obstacle in federated learning, causing divergence between locally trained networks and unstable convergence of the global model. We address these issues by introducing a novel regularization approach that operates at the architectural level: multiple auxiliary branches are constructed within each local model by grafting together local and global subnetworks at several distinct levels, and online knowledge distillation is employed to align the representations of the main pathway with those of the resulting hybrid auxiliary pathways. Without introducing any additional communication overhead, the proposed method integrates conveniently into a wide range of federated learning frameworks and substantially improves the robustness of the global model under non-iid data distributions. Extensive empirical evaluation demonstrates that the proposed method achieves notable gains in both accuracy and efficiency relative to prior approaches. Code is publicly accessible via our project page.

author: Chavez
title: Knowledge Distillation Without Training Data for Compressing Deep Neural Networks
abstract: Model compression techniques have made it possible to reduce the size of large neural networks to a small fraction of their original footprint while preserving most or all of their predictive accuracy. A fundamental limitation shared by all such techniques, however, is their dependence on the original training data — data that may be unavailable due to the prohibitive scale of the dataset, or because making it accessible raises privacy or safety concerns, as is commonly the case in biometrics applications. We introduce the proposed method, a data-free approach to knowledge distillation that is capable of compressing deep neural networks trained on large-scale datasets down to a fraction of their original size, requiring only a small amount of supplementary metadata distributed alongside a pretrained model. In addition, we investigate several varieties of metadata compatible with the proposed method and analyze the tradeoffs that arise from each choice.

author: Mckay
title: Efficient Compression of Large-scale Language Models via Data Augmentation-Enhanced Distillation
abstract: Impressive empirical gains have recently been achieved by large-scale language models, yet these advances come with substantially heavier computational requirements, higher energy demands, and increased latency during inference — factors that severely limit deployment on platforms with constrained memory and processing capacity. Knowledge distillation (KD) offers a well-established mechanism for compressing such oversized models. That said, large-scale neural network systems are susceptible to memorizing individual training instances, which causes unstable predictions under even minor shifts in data distribution. A further difficulty is that, when task-specific data is scarce, the student model has limited occasions to extract meaningful guidance from the teacher model. The proposed method addresses both of these problems through a data-agnostic distillation framework that incorporates mixup — a straightforward yet computationally efficient data augmentation strategy — to equip the distilled model with improved generalization. Specifically, beyond learning from the original training examples, the student model is also trained to replicate the teacher's outputs on linearly interpolated pairs of examples. Under reasonable assumptions, we provide a theoretical analysis showing that the proposed method yields a reduced discrepancy between generalization error and empirical error. Evaluation on the GLUE benchmark confirms this, with the proposed method delivering consistent and substantial improvements over standard KD training while surpassing several strong competing baselines. The benefits of the approach are further corroborated by experiments in a data-limited regime and by a series of ablation studies.

author: Liu
title: Vision-Language Knowledge Distillation for Equipping CLIP with Multimodal Generation Capabilities
abstract: Dual-stream architectures such as CLIP, trained via large-scale vision-language pre-training (VLP) on massive image-text pair corpora, have demonstrated clear superiority across a range of multimodal alignment tasks. However, because of their weak text encoder, these models lack the ability to perform multimodal generative tasks. To address this limitation, we introduce a method that incorporates a textual pre-trained language model (PLM) into a dual-stream VLP model through vision-language knowledge distillation (VLKD), thereby endowing it with multimodal generation capability. Relative to pre-training from scratch, VLKD requires substantially less data and computation. Our experiments demonstrate strong zero-shot performance on multimodal generation tasks including image captioning and open-ended visual question answering. Specifically, on the VQAv2 dataset, the proposed method achieves 44.5% zero-shot accuracy, exceeding the previous state-of-the-art zero-shot model while using 7× fewer parameters. In addition, following VLKD, the PLM retains its original textual language understanding and generation abilities, rendering our model effective for both unimodal and multimodal tasks.

author: Mason
title: Student Network Training Through Feature Embedding Techniques
abstract: Storage and computational demands of deep convolutional neural networks, despite their widespread adoption across many applications, render them unsuitable for deployment on mobile devices. Knowledge distillation addresses this by transferring knowledge from a well-trained, heavyweight teacher network to guide the optimization of a compact student network. Conventional teacher-student approaches typically require extra fully-connected layers to align the intermediate layers of the teacher and student networks, introducing a substantial number of auxiliary parameters. The method proposed here, by contrast, transfers information from teacher to student without adding any new variables to be optimized. Framing the teacher-student paradigm through the lens of feature embedding, the proposed method applies a locality preserving loss to guide the student network toward producing low-dimensional features that retain the intrinsic properties of the corresponding high-dimensional features extracted by the teacher network. As a result, the compact student network naturally preserves performance comparable to that of the teacher network. A theoretical analysis is offered to establish the lower computational complexity of the proposed method. Evaluations conducted on benchmark datasets using well-trained networks demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art teacher-student learning methods with respect to both computational and storage complexity.

author: White
title: Lightweight Generative Adversarial Networks for Image Translation via Knowledge Distillation
abstract: Although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have found broad application across a wide range of image-to-image translation tasks, their substantial computational and memory requirements make deployment on mobile devices highly impractical. Existing network compression techniques have been developed primarily for visual recognition tasks and have not addressed generation tasks. Drawing inspiration from knowledge distillation, a student generator with a reduced parameter count is trained to inherit both low-level and high-level information from a heavier teacher generator. To strengthen the student generator's capacity, a student discriminator is introduced to quantify the discrepancies among real images and images produced by both the student and teacher generators. This formulation gives rise to an adversarial learning procedure that jointly optimizes the student generator and student discriminator. Through qualitative and quantitative experiments conducted on benchmark datasets, the proposed method is shown to be capable of producing portable generative models that maintain strong performance.

author: Gaines
title: Task-Specific BERT Compression via Differentiable Neural Architecture Search
abstract: Pre-trained language models of substantial scale, BERT being a prominent example, have demonstrated strong effectiveness across a wide range of natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, their enormous number of parameters presents a barrier to deployment in latency-sensitive applications where computational resources are constrained. Prior compression approaches reduce BERT to smaller models in a task-agnostic manner, producing a single compressed model applied uniformly across all downstream tasks. Recognizing both the need for and the advantages of compressing BERT in a task-aware fashion, we introduce the proposed method, which employs differentiable Neural Architecture Search to automatically derive task-adaptive small models tailored to individual tasks. A task-oriented knowledge distillation loss is integrated to guide the architecture search, alongside an efficiency-aware loss that acts as a search constraint, together yielding a favorable balance between effectiveness and efficiency in task-adaptive BERT compression. Experiments conducted on multiple NLP benchmarks show that the task-adaptive compressed models produced by the proposed method achieve 12.7x to 29.3x reductions in inference time and 11.5x to 17.0x reductions in parameter size relative to BERT, while sustaining comparable performance.

author: Harrell
title: Every Client Counts: Federated Learning Across Devices with Heterogeneous Capabilities
abstract: As a privacy-preserving framework for building global models from distributed, decentralized data, federated learning (FL) has emerged as a critical paradigm in modern machine learning. A common assumption in existing FL approaches is that all participating clients are capable of training the global model; however, client devices in practical deployments differ substantially in their available computing power. Powerful models such as BERT have demonstrated remarkable achievements across AI tasks, yet deploying them in heterogeneous FL settings that include weak clients remains a significant challenge. Naive remedies—such as excluding weak clients entirely or constraining the model size to accommodate all devices—introduce their own shortcomings: dropped clients become underrepresented, while a universally small model suffers from reduced accuracy due to both data loss and insufficient representational capacity. To address these issues, the proposed method takes a client-inclusive approach in which models of varying sizes are distributed according to each client's computational capability, with larger models assigned to stronger clients and smaller models to weaker ones. A mechanism for sharing knowledge across these multiple local models of differing sizes is also introduced, enabling all clients to contribute to FL training and allowing the resulting global model to retain high capacity and strong performance. Furthermore, the proposed method incorporates a momentum-based knowledge distillation strategy that more effectively transfers knowledge from large models running on powerful clients to small models running on weak clients. Comprehensive experiments conducted on a wide range of real-world benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed method in producing accurate global models under heterogeneous device conditions within the FL framework.

author: Evans
title: Distilling Efficient Evaluation Metrics for Machine Translation
abstract: Trained metrics such as BLEURT or COMET, which frame translation quality assessment as a regression task and draw representations from multilingual pre-trained models like mBERT or XLM-RoBERTa, have become increasingly prevalent in machine translation and multilingual text generation research. Evidence from related tasks, however, indicates that such models tend to perform best at large scales, making them expensive and impractical for routine evaluation purposes. Using WMT Metrics Shared Task data, we examine how model capacity and multilinguality interact in RemBERT, a state-of-the-art multilingual language model. Through a sequence of experiments, we first establish that model size constitutes a genuine bottleneck for cross-lingual transfer, and then show that this bottleneck can be addressed via distillation, combining synthetic data generation with the transfer of knowledge from a single teacher to several students trained across related languages. Compared to vanilla fine-tuning, the proposed method achieves improvements of up to 10.5%, and with only one third of RemBERT's parameters it retains 92.6% of its performance.

author: Fowler
title: Self-Supervised Knowledge Transfer via Distillation for Compact Visual Encoders
abstract: This work addresses the challenge of self-supervised learning when the target architecture is a small model. Our motivation stems from empirical observations showing that contrastive self-supervised learning, despite its substantial progress on large model training, fails to generalize effectively to small models. To tackle this, we introduce a learning paradigm in which a larger network acting as a teacher transfers its representational knowledge to a compact architecture acting as a student, entirely within a self-supervised framework. Rather than training the student encoder directly on unlabeled data, we supervise it to replicate the distribution of similarity scores that the teacher assigns across a collection of instances. The proposed method yields dramatic gains for small networks on downstream tasks.
